The search giant is giving schools more control over AI, but there's a big catch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Google says it's giving schools more control over AI, but there's a meaningful catch that parents can't ignore. Schools that want to keep AI out of the classroom will also have to give up Google Search through student accounts.

In a Tuesday announcement, Google said it will disable access to several products, including Gemini and Google Search, for K–12 student accounts unless school administrators turn them on.

But there's one thing schools won't be able to do: Keep Google Search while blocking its built-in AI features.

"If a school is not comfortable with that and simply wants AI off, then they have the choice to not have Search on at all," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president of education, told Chalkbeat.

The changes, expected to roll out in early 2027, could leave school districts choosing between allowing AI-generated answers in Search or finding another way for students to research their homework.

Google has spent years integrating AI into its search engine, most visibly through AI Overviews, which provide generated summaries above traditional search results.

Now, those features are becoming a sticking point for schools that want students to research independently without relying on AI-generated answers.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

"Search and AI are deeply integrated," Chris Phillips, Google's vice president for education, told The New York Times.

According to Phillips, students in schools that prohibit AI entirely will not have access to Google Search through their school accounts. Instead, they'll see a message indicating that the service is unavailable.

The restriction applies to school-managed accounts under the new controls,

Google has also made it clear that administrators can enable individual products, including Gemini and Google Search, rather than accepting every AI service as a package. But the problem is much greater because schools still cannot offer an entirely AI-free version of Google Search.

Alongside the changes to school controls, Google is expanding Guided Learning, an AI-powered feature designed to help students understand subjects rather than simply giving them answers.

Guided Learning is already available in Gemini, and Google announced that the feature is now available globally in Google Classroom.

The company is also bringing similar capabilities to Google Search, beginning with a pilot in selected U.S. schools later this month.

For example, a student who searches for help with a physics problem might receive questions and explanations that guide them through the solution rather than an immediate final answer.

Someone researching a book report could receive prompts encouraging them to think through the material. Google calls this approach "productive struggle," the idea that students learn more when they work through challenges rather than immediately receiving solutions.

In Google Classroom, teachers can assign Guided Learning activities based on class materials and receive feedback about where students might need additional support.

Google says its research shows that Guided Learning can improve learning outcomes. However, the effectiveness of these tools in everyday classrooms will depend on how students use them and how well the AI avoids simply completing assignments for them.

There are already questions about those safeguards. In testing reported by The New York Times, the consumer version of Guided Learning produced a detailed essay when given an Advanced Placement history prompt. Google says the school version includes additional restrictions.

The changes come amid growing concerns about how AI tools affect children and teenagers.

AI can be useful for explaining difficult concepts, brainstorming ideas and helping students study. But educators also worry that students may become too dependent on chatbots, use them to complete assignments or trust answers that aren't always accurate.

In September, New York City and Los Angeles, two of the country's largest school districts, introduced restrictions on student access to generative AI tools on school devices.

Some school officials have specifically wanted the ability to disable Google's AI Overviews while preserving conventional web searches.

Google's new policy does not provide that option. The company is reversing an earlier decision to enable certain AI features by default in Google Classroom for schools that had already permitted Gemini access.

That reversal gives administrators more control over which Google AI products students can use. But it stops short of letting schools completely separate Google Search from its built-in AI features.

For families, the most important thing to understand is that these changes are not taking effect immediately. Google says that it will share more details with schools in the coming months, with the new controls expected to arrive in early 2027.

Whether a student loses access to Google Search through their school account will depend on the choices made by their district or school administrators.

Schools can enable specific Google products individually, but those that want to keep AI entirely out of Google Search may need to consider alternative search engines or research tools.

Parents concerned about AI in their children's classrooms can ask their schools which Google services are currently enabled, whether students can access Gemini, and how the district plans to handle the upcoming changes.

It's also worth asking whether students will be using Guided Learning and what oversight teachers will have over those interactions.

Why my offline zakat app ships a Hijri lookup table instead of a calendar algorithm

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

I'm the developer of Zakat, a small offline Android app (Kotlin + Jetpack Compose + Room) that helps Muslims track the zakat they owe each year. Zakat falls due once per lunar year, so the whole app depends on one question: what Gregorian date is "1 Dhul Qi'dah 1448"?

Android does have options: java.time.chrono.HijrahDate, and ICU's IslamicCalendar with civil, tabular and Umm al-Qura variants. I didn't use them, for four reasons:

The rule in the codebase is short: the app never computes a Hijri date at runtime. Every date comes from a table lookup.

A small Python script, run on my machine and never shipped, uses the hijridate package (Umm al-Qura) to write the Gregorian date of the first day of every Hijri month from 1440 to 1500 AH:

That is 61 years × 12 months plus one sentinel row: 733 entries, about 52 KB of JSON, covering 11 Sep 2018 to 16 Nov 2077.

1. The table does not store month lengths. A month's length is the gap between its first day and the next month's first day. The table can't disagree with itself, because it only says each fact once. The sentinel row (1 Muharram 1501) exists only so the last real month has a "next month" to measure against.

Across the table there are 389 thirty-day months and 343 twenty-nine-day months. Remember that ratio.

2. The JVM module and the APK read the same file. The JSON lives in core/src/main/resources, and the app module adds that folder as an asset source, so there is one file and no copy to drift:

The reverse lookup (Gregorian → Hijri) is a binary search over the month starts. It is only used once, to suggest the user's first year; after that, each year follows from the previous one.

Umm al-Qura is a calculated calendar. If your mosque announces Ramadan from a local sighting, its first day can differ from the table by a day. So a per-year due-date override always wins over the table:

The app does not try to know better than the user's own community.

The due-date override was a normal date picker, so nothing stopped a user from picking, say, 27 March 2098, which is outside the table.

The result: the app crashed on every launch, and the only way out was clearing the app's data. That is the worst outcome for an app whose whole job is keeping your records.

The fix was tested on a real upgrade path: install the old build, plant an out-of-range date in its database, watch it crash-loop, install the fixed build over it, and check that it opens.

Settings store the anniversary as a (month, day) pair, for example 30 Ramadan. When the user starts a new zakat year, the app resolves that pair in the new Hijri year.

In the Umm al-Qura table, Ramadan 1448 (starting 8 Feb 2027) has 29 days, and so does Dhul Qi'dah 1448. resolve(HijriDate(1448, 9, 30)) correctly threw, because that day does not exist. But it threw inside a viewModelScope.launch with no handler, so the process died.

The bug was not in the table. It was a mix-up between two meanings:

So now there are two functions, and the name tells you which one you're calling:

The ViewModel also stopped trusting that nothing can go wrong:

Note the CancellationException rethrow. A blanket catch (e: Exception) in a coroutine also catches cancellation, which quietly breaks structured concurrency.

Before these fixes, my tests checked a set of anchor dates: 1 Dhul Qi'dah of every year, plus a few others, against the spec. They were all correct, and they still missed both bugs. Anchors prove the data is right. They say nothing about the edges.

The table is finite: 732 real months. When your domain is that small, test all of it instead of samples. These run in milliseconds on the JVM:

And the one that walks the entire table. For every month of every year, a day-30 anniversary must land inside coverage, and on that same month's last day:

A last test checks that covers() and hijriDateContaining() agree at both edges of the table. Neither bug can come back without a red build.

The broader lesson: every "this can't happen" in date code is a month with 29 days that you haven't met yet. Both crashes were in code with tests. They just weren't the right tests.

Disclosure: I built this app. It's free, with no ads, no account and no analytics, and it's in English, French and Arabic (full RTL): Zakat on Google Play. It's a calculation aid, not a fatwa.

A question for you: if you've shipped anything with Hijri dates, how did you handle the gap between Umm al-Qura and local moon sighting? I'd love to hear how others approach it.

Apple warned that AI agents could act in ways it didn't authorize

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Apple's 10-K lists reputational harm, regulatory action and legal liability among risks tied to its AI efforts

David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Apple $AAPL warned in its annual report on Tuesday that AI agents, whether built by the company or by third parties, may take actions that were "not directed, instructed or authorized."

The 10-K, for the fiscal year ended Sept. 26, says such agents can operate on their own, for instance by reaching systems they may not have permission to enter, running or changing code, sending messages and finalizing purchases. Apple said the agents may exceed permissions, defy instructions, circumvent security measures or be manipulated through malicious inputs.

The company said agents may conceal actions, withhold or manipulate information, or generate deceptive outputs. Many of the technologies are nondeterministic, so their behavior can be difficult to anticipate, control, test and audit, and errors can compound across multistep workflows, Apple said. Some consequences, such as deleting data or completing transactions, may be difficult or impossible to reverse.

Apple said it may have only limited power to supervise and direct third-party AI agents, and that its policies and controls may fail to keep pace with advancing technology. The company said these issues could expose it to reputational and competitive harm, regulatory action and legal liability.

The filing says AI agents that require access to personal data create privacy and data security concerns that could erode customer trust. It describes legal and regulatory frameworks for AI as divergent and evolving, and says Apple may have to spend significant sums to adapt to new laws.

Apple has no agentic AI product, according to CNBC. On an earnings call on Monday, CEO John Ternus said agentic tools look promising for users but that Apple wants them to know what access they are granting. "We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy," Ternus said.

Last month, Apple announced changes to full disk access on Macs, with the aim of lowering "risks related to this level of access" for AI agents, according to CNBC.

Meta $META launched its Muse agent on Sept. 8, and OpenAI introduced its Dots agents at its DevDay event, as AI agents reached a broader consumer audience. Amazon $AMZN blocked Muse from its store and said it never authorized the agent.

In another case, a Muse agent managing the Facebook Marketplace listings of tech reviewer Matt Robb replied to a buyer as Robb, agreed on a price and sent his Toronto home address. Robb had clicked "Allow Always" on a permissions prompt. Meta said it would make the prompt clearer.

French Museum’s ‘Wanted’ Poster Campaign for Stolen Art Leads to Return of Missing 17th-Century Dutch Painting

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Thanks to an inventive “Wanted” campaign by the Musée des Beaux-Arts d’Orléans in France, aimed at tracking down hundreds of WWII-era looted artworks, one painting has just been found, the museum’s director told ARTnews.

A 17th-century painting by Dutch artist Willem Cornelisz Duyster, titled Un Buveur (The Drinker) and stolen in 1940 from the Orléans museum, was located last month at an auction house in Switzerland and is on its way back home to the French museum, Le Journal de l’Art reported earlier. Related Articles Italy Looks to Join Its European Counterparts With Restitution Legislation Swiss Government to Fund Research into Holdings of Cultural Artifacts

After being presented with the evidence of the theft, “the possessor of the work immediately agreed to restitute it at no cost,” said Olivia Voisin, the museum’s director. The painting is currently being held in customs at the French border. Voisin said the museum was able to find the missing painting thanks to a recent campaign that uses a bit of humor to spread awareness about some 350 artworks that were plundered from the Musée Paul Fourché, an annex of the Beaux-Arts museum, after the city was attacked by Nazis in June 1940. It is believed people on both sides of the conflict took advantage of the opportunity to ransack the museum.

The poster campaign features the words “WANTED” written in chunky, all caps in American Old Western font, across a selection of black-and-white images of the museum’s lost artworks. These have been shared on social media, the museum website, and other news platforms, and are bolstered by a two-year-old digital catalog of the stolen works.

So far, it seems to be working. One local from Orléans, who saw the “Wanted” posters, decided to spend his free time searching for the missing paintings. “He wanted to help us, and that was the goal of the campaign: that these searches are shared or collective,” said Voisin.

While randomly sifting through online auctions, the unnamed Orléans resident came across Un Buveur in a catalog for an October 17 sale at the Gloggner auction house in Lucerne. It was estimated to be worth about $3,400 and thought to be a study of the original. It depicts a jolly scene of a seated man, dressed in contemporary garb and holding out an empty glass; he raises his other arm and appears to be caught in midsentence.

The museum was tipped off about the curious painting and contacted the auction house, which immediately cooperated and “was very transparent throughout,” said Voisin, noting that attitudes have changed in that regard. After she presented the painting’s holder with an image of the original superimposed on a digital image of their painting, they saw it was a perfect match. He had purchased it from a London auction house in the 1990s.

“He immediately proposed to restitute the painting,” she said. “It was pretty natural for him to return it, because he felt that he had been able to enjoy it for 35 years, and it was time for it to go home.”

The painting is considered one of Duyster’s finest, and in many ways represents the museum’s stolen collection, which once held several similar Dutch paintings from the 17th century showing scenes of revelry. However, the painting appears to be damaged by several layers of overpainting and cleaning attempts. If in good condition, Voisin estimated it to be worth between €25,000 and €30,000 ($28,000 to $33,600).

The Orléans museum has been trying for years to recover the artworks lost during World War II, with little luck. To date, 424 paintings are still missing from its collection, counting additional paintings that have gone missing or were stolen at different periods. They include works by Édouard Manet, Hans Holbein the Younger, Anthony van Dyck, Lorenzo Costa, and one attributed to Raphael’s Renaissance workshop. Since the creation of the digital catalog and the “Wanted” poster campaign, four paintings, including Un Buveur, have been returned over the past few years.

Google will disable Search for students unless schools accept AI features in ‘Guided Learning’ push

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Google is today launching new AI settings for schools, but with the big catch that Search is fully disabled if AI features are turned off entirely.

In a blog post today, Google says it is “focused on building technology responsibly to help students thrive” and, as such, will tailor its AI efforts to help students. “Guided Learning” in Gemini, Search, and Classroom will include helping students “work through problems without skipping straight to answers.”

…if a student pastes a complex physics problem or asks for help writing a book report in Search, they’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer.

That’s launching in a pilot program this month in select US schools, with Guided Learning in Google Classroom launching globally today. Google describes this as a “1-1 study tool, anchored in class material to help [students] stay on task” while also giving the teacher insights into how their class is handling the material.

Beyond this new Guided Learning push, Google also says that it will now turn off “Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search” for K-12 student accounts by default “until school administrators explicitly turn them on.”

As The New York Times points out, having those features fully off has a big side effect: it cuts students off from Google Search entirely.

Google says that this is because Search and AI “are deeply integrated” and confirms that students in schools with AI features turned off (which, to reiterate, is now the default setting) “will not have access to search.”

As a reminder, Google Search’s AI features can largely be turned off using a simple modifier.

Google’s post says that the “goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit.” Yet, speaking to The New York Times, Google further explained that two options will be available to schools in “early 2027,” one that has AI Overviews and other AI features turned on, the other with Guided Learning in their place, leaving schools with no choice other than to accept AI features or give up access to Google Search for their students entirely.

NYT points out repeatedly that Google’s prior AI pushes in schools have been met with fierce opposition from educators and parents alike.

Deep inside a Spanish cave, archaeologists found at least 120 Latin inscriptions, and five of them honor a goddess called ‘the Lady’

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

At least 120 Latin inscriptions in Cova Dones, Spain, name a goddess called Domina, the Lady, and point to women taking an active part in her cult.

One chamber of Cova Dones, a cave in Millares in Valencia province, now holds at least 120 Latin inscriptions. Teams from the universities of Alicante and Zaragoza recorded them during fieldwork in May and June 2026.

When the room was first explored in 2024, about 15 had been logged.

Five of the texts are vows to Domina, “the Lady,” a goddess the visitors addressed with reverence. Several of the names read so far are women’s. The team calls the results preliminary, and many texts are still being read.

The researchers call the room the Roman Sanctuary. It sits more than 650 feet (200 meters) from the entrance, according to the University of Alicante.

Most of the texts are believed to date to the 1st and 2nd centuries AD, and they cover the walls and the ceiling. Small natural pools on the floor, known as gours, catch water from the galleries, and visitors dropped offerings into them.

That first campaign also yielded a coin from the reign of Emperor Claudius. Someone had wedged it as an offering between a fissure and a stalactite in the ceiling, and in a team photo Xabier Garín Artázcoz points at the crack. Trinidad Pasíes Oviedo of the Valencia Museum of Prehistory recovered and conserved the coin.

The January 2025 announcement from the University of Alicante placed the room among the deepest known Roman inscription sites in Iberia, second only to Cueva del Puente in Burgos and possibly Cueva de Román de Clunia.

This year’s readings were done by two epigraphy specialists. Silvia Alfayé teaches ancient history at the University of Zaragoza, and Sergio García-Dils lectures at UNED in Seville. García-Dils also directs the Spanish School of Speleology.

According to Alfayé, five votive texts show that women “played an active role in her cult.” Three of them carry the word MALACI. In a release dated July 27, the University of Alicante called it an unpublished epithet for a goddess not known until now.

García-Dils noted that the texts are packed into one marked-off part of the cave, well away from the entrance. To him that “strongly suggests the existence of a well-organised and structured cult” with a named deity, not scattered visits.

The University of Southampton, where Aitor Ruiz-Redondo is also based, put out the English release on October 20. It says early readings suggest some women wrote their vows themselves, without a go-between.

Until now, the Roman cave sanctuary with the largest known set of inscriptions was La Griega, with 107. One of them names a woman.

The 2026 team logged objects on the chamber floor, among them two bronze rings found under the inscribed rock. There were two bronze rings, a bracelet, chalice-shaped cups, spindle whorls, bits of pottery and animal bones.

The whorls came up in numbers. Virginia Barciela co-leads the project with Ruiz-Redondo and teaches prehistory at Alicante. She said the whorls probably point to offerings of spindles, a textile tool tied to women in antiquity.

She also brought up the first written name of the site, Cova de les Dones, meaning Cave of the Women. That name may hold “the fossilised memory of a place long associated with women,” she said, or with female spirits.

Alfayé said the goddess’s title may have to do with water. Water shrines existed elsewhere in the ancient world, such as a circular water shrine at Pelusium in northern Sinai.

The inscriptions are extremely difficult to see with the naked eye. So the team photographed the surfaces for high-resolution photogrammetric models and read the texts on those.

That work turned up inscriptions no one had seen. It also split apart lines that earlier readers had taken as one text.

Jorge Angás and Carlos Valladares, from the IPH institute in Zaragoza and the DigHER project, ran the geomatics side. Javier Velaza Frías, a Latin professor in Barcelona, leads the study of the Roman inscriptions. Víctor Sabaté Vidal of the University of Valencia has also contributed to the project.

Latin wishes turn up on other Roman objects too, for instance openwork glass cups carved with drinking wishes in Greek or Latin.

In a Roman underground sanctuary, finding texts and offerings together in place is exceptionally rare, says the Southampton release.

Ruiz-Redondo, Barciela and archaeologist Ximo Martorell published the first results in 2023. In the journal Antiquity they described over 100 Paleolithic paintings and engravings. Some are older than 24,000 years.

Pottery from the Iron Age had already led archaeologists in the 1960s to class it as an Iberian sanctuary. In 2025 the team logged more than 100 stalagmites that people had modified on purpose.

For that kind of find, the University of Alicante ranks the cave second in the world, after Saint-Marcel in France.

Ruiz-Redondo said people may have kept returning for “its permanent water supply,” its landscape or its easy access.

At La Pasiega, Maltravieso and Ardales, red marks have been dated to more than 64,000 years ago.

Alfayé and her colleagues are still working on the goddess’s title. For now the team has not said who Domina was or what MALACI means. Many inscriptions are still being read, and much of the cave is unstudied, so 120 is a minimum.

The DONARQ project started in 2023 with money from the Generalitat Valenciana and the British Academy. In September 2026 the sanctuary was shortlisted for a National Geographic +Historia readers’ prize. Public voting closed on October 12.

This year the regional Pla Restaura program and the Millares town council are paying for more work. The money goes to the cave’s access and entrance, safety measures, a digital twin and a catalog of the Paleolithic images. The company Arquivolta Patrimoni i Societat is coordinating it, and virtual visits should follow.

Among those offerings, two bronze rings sat on the surface right below the inscribed rock.

The information was obtained from the University of Southampton , the University of Alicante and the University of Zaragoza.

Warner Music Buys Back Part of German Distributor Zebralution, Expanding Reach in Europe

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

The pioneering digital distributor of music and audiobooks was sold by WMG in 2017 but now returns with enhanced resources.

By Elizabeth Dilts Marshall

Warner Music Group (WMG) said Tuesday (Nov. 3) it had acquired indie record label distributor Zebralution Music GmbH from Bookwire, bringing back part of the Zebralution company it owned for a decade and expanding the major’s reach into the business of serving Germany and Europe.

Zebralution Music is a spinoff of Zebralution Gmbh, which Bookwire acquired from the German performance rights organization GEMA in March 2026. In a press release announcing the Bookwire acquisition at the time, Bookwire described Zebralution as among the first big digital distributors of music, audiobooks, e-books and podcasts, with more than 1,500 label and publisher clients globally. Terms of the deal were not disclosed.

WMG acquired Zebralution in 2007 and sold it in 2017 to its founders Kurt Thielen, Sascha Lazimbat, Christof Ellinghaus and Konrad von Löhneysen. Founded in 2003, Zebralution distributed a catalog of 500,000-plus tracks, albums and videos to hundreds of digital services worldwide at the time WMG sold it.

The reacquisition follows WMG’s April deal to buy B2B music distribution platform Revelator and further expands the reach and services offered through WMG and its distribution and services offerings housed under ADA. Zebralution Music label clients gain access to WMG’s technology, distribution, analytics and financial tools. The company’s now co-CEOs von Löhneysen and Lazimbat will remain with the company “to align strategic operations,” according to a statement.

“This is an exciting new chapter for Zebralution Music, but for our label partners and the people we work with every day, it will very much be business as usual,” Lazimbat said in a statement. “We’ll continue to operate with the same team, the same relationships … What does change is the additional technology and resources now available to us, which will help us build on what we have already achieved.”

Von Löhneysen, whose own label, Embassy of Music, is a Zebralution client, echoed the sentiment that customers should expect “the same people, the same approach and the same independence they’ve always valued.”

Niels Walboomers, president of Warner Music Central Europe, said WMG was drawn to Zebralution’s regional expertise and world-class capabilities.

“Konrad and Sascha have built one of the most trusted homes for independent music in Europe,” Walboomers said.

CrowdStrike is rolling out an AI kill switch to stop rogue AI agents

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Falcon Guardian feature requires an administrator to trigger it, and endpoint-level termination is planned

CrowdStrike $CRWD launched an AI kill switch on Tuesday that gives security teams a way to shut down rogue AI agents, prevent them from starting up again and sever their access to the enterprise network, the company said.

The feature is part of Falcon Guardian, CrowdStrike's product for securing AI agents. An authorized administrator triggers the action, and every step is recorded in an audit trail, the company said. Falcon Guardian policy keeps a terminated agent from relaunching on the targeted host or host group.

At launch, the Falcon sensor halts agents at the AI Gateway. Termination on the endpoint is planned for a later release, according to CrowdStrike.

"Every organization is racing to get more out of AI, and every week we see agents chain steps together, hit an obstacle, and take actions they were never authorized to take," CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas said in a statement.

CrowdStrike also announced other Falcon Guardian updates. Endpoint network inspection is generally available for Windows, with Mac in early access. The company also introduced an integration with Anthropic that runs the Falcon sensor inside the Claude Cowork virtual machine. CrowdStrike said it plans to acquire Fiddler to add agent observability.

Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard told CNBC that, for customers running the Falcon platform, the tool functions as a simple on-off toggle. It can spot what agents are doing inside a customer's environment, he said, but judging whether that behavior is harmless or hostile falls to a person.

"If you kill a process at the root, and we have that level of access at the root … it's very binary," Bernard said, according to CNBC. "You either kill the AI and the agent, or you don't, and then you report on that."

CrowdStrike also plans to acquire AI security testing firm Dreadnode, according to CNBC.

The launch follows legislative efforts to require shutdown capabilities in AI systems. Reps. Ted Lieu and Nathaniel Moran introduced the Kill Switch Act after OpenAI disclosed an incident in which rogue models circumvented a sandboxed testing environment and accessed Hugging Face. The bill would require AI companies to maintain the ability to shut down, throttle or suspend their models.

Critics contend that building an emergency stop mechanism would prove too unwieldy given the number of systems, data centers and sophisticated AI models it would have to span, according to CNBC.

Phantom Blade Zero Meets God of War Ragnarök in Upcoming Steam Action Game Hit

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

There's more God of War here than expected

Right now, the gaming world is obsessed with Phantom Blade Zero. S-Game’s Wuxia-inspired action game landed as one of the highest-rated games of 2026 and immediately tore up the charts on Steam, cracking 800,000 concurrent players on launch weekend. I’m enjoying Phantom Blade Zero, even if it does have a few too many parries for my taste. But it’s primarily made me more excited about a similar, promising game I briefly played earlier this year: Tides of Annihilation.

Tides of Annihilation is a forthcoming contender in a specific subgenre of games largely developed in China that defy easy characterization but have been rapidly growing in popularity, thanks to hits like Phantom Blade Zero and Black Myth: Wukong. Earlier this year, at Gamescom 2026, I played about 45 minutes of what appeared to be an early level. It ruled. (Tides made Polygon’s list of the best games at Gamescom 2026.) It’s a little bit character action game, a little bit Soulslike. But in many ways, it’s more in conversation with God of War (2018) and its sequel, God of War Ragnarök, than with anything out of FromSoftware’s haunted halls.

In fact, here’s a line directly from my notes: “Hot girl god of war???”

There is simply no way around it: Gwendolyn, the main character of Tides of Annihilation, is stunning. This has become some matter of debate among the game’s community.

In July, 2025 Game Awards winner Jennifer English, initially slated to play Gwendolyn, dropped out of the role, citing health concerns. Eclipse Glow Games quickly revealed her replacement as Angela Sant’Albano (best known for her role as Grace Ashcroft in Resident Evil Requiem), and around the same time, redesigned Gwendolyn’s facial features. “Do we all agree that she looks beautiful?” reads one top Reddit post from the time. You’ll never believe this but: No. No they did not all agree.

Hands-on with Tides, I can say that Gwendolyn’s model doesn’t look cheap, rushed, or like “every mmo Korean AI slop model,” to quote one Reddit user. She looks great — like an actual human being rather than an anime figurine tucked into the corner of an IKEA bookshelf. And yes, she happens to be conventionally attractive. But Gwendolyn’s character design isn’t played for sheer objectification, like, say, genre contemporary Stellar Blade treats its main character Eve. The camera never lingers uncomfortably at creep-shot angles, nor are scenes framed like peep shows. That said, because I only played a small portion of Tides, who knows what the full game will be like. But given how much discussion Gwendolyn’s character model has already generated, this will almost certainly be a hot topic upon its release.

Anyway. The game. Tides of Annihilation’s fantasy elements are inspired by Arthurian legend (there’s another God of War nod for you). Set in modern-day London, a mysterious entity called the Fog has wrought apocalyptic destruction, as tree roots a foot wide snake their way through the city. Rage-red crystals pepper the buildings that remain, as do a variety of Gothic-inspired humanoids and fantasy creatures. Gwendolyn appears to be the only person left alive who possesses any way to resist the Fog, and seeks a way to undo its damage.

On a basic level, combat in Tides is a lot like many other flashy, fast-paced character action games: You can perform light attacks, heavy attacks, and various combos that string both together. You can jump, dodge, and parry, and variously colored glints of enemy attacks will indicate which of those defensive moves you should make. Enemies have stagger bars that you whittle down, stunning them when depleted. And finishing moves tend to be stylish as hell; in one, Gwendolyn ripped a 15-foot-long spear out of her enemy’s hand, then leapt into the air before careening it through her foe. But the biggest gimmick in combat is the addition of equippable knights.

Knights are avatars, inspired by the famous Knights of the Round Table, who accompany Gwendolyn at all times. You can use these knights to “enhance” your attacks; though Gwendolyn is always a speedy fighter, knights can alter your moveset to be more defensive, to prioritize staggering, or apparently to even introduce game-changing abilities like a time-stopping mechanic. Though I only was able to use two in my demo, Gwendolyn can unlock up to ten knights in the full game. (Historians disagree about how many knights actually sat at the table.)

These knights are also critical parts of the 3D Metroidvania aspects of Tides. My preview was largely located in a single area, in and around a museum of Egyptian history. To explore the museum fully, I needed to use my knights. Bors had to fire his bow to create ziplines across wide chasms, while Palamedes needed to smash down fractured walls and reposition bookshelves between balconies, creating makeshift bridges. It’s all reminiscent of the ways Kratos and Atreus navigate the nine realms of Norse myth: merrily moving along until you need to tap Triangle to shoot the thing. All the combat prowess in the world, and you still can’t navigate it alone.

That’s not all the God of War on display here. For instance, at one point, my path forward was blocked off by a wall of red crystals. I later earned the ability to pick up an explosive red sphere that looked like a grapefruit; tossing it at the wall of crystals caused them to shatter, a mechanic that’s an almost 1:1 recreation of God of War Ragnarök’s Shatter Crystals.

I say this not as a knock on derivative game design but rather as a compliment to an evolving niche of popular video games. You don’t need to closely follow the industry to see that the Chinese action game scene is popping off in a real way in recent years, with a string of slick projects that each have a distinct feel and style. Tides of Annihilation comes on the heels of Black Myth and Phantom Blade, but is also on most-anticipated lists alongside Blood Message, one of the most promising games out of Summer Game Fest 2026. (This is to say nothing of the behemoth that is miHoYo, which has its own game in this vein with the forthcoming Nodusfall.)

A weekly cheat sheet to what you’ll eventually love to play. No buying, no commitment — just saving for later.

These games all neatly fit into what my colleague Oli Welsh has deemed the “outsider AAA” game — highly polished games from well-funded studios that nevertheless outside of the Nintendo-Xbox-PlayStation Bermuda Triangle. These games aren’t quite born from the halls of megawatt funding, but they’re no less excellent — nor held in lower esteem. Black Myth: Wukong nabbed a Game Awards nomination in 2024. Phantom Blade Zero is in the conversation for 2026, though faces a steep uphill climb against the likes of You Know What. For many reasons, least of all that it does not yet have a release year, I would not even begin to wager a formal prediction about Tides of Annihilation, let alone in writing. Then again, you don’t need to see the tides change to know that they will.

Tides of Annihilation will be released for PlayStation 5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X.

A new breed of reactionary studio from outside gaming's traditional heartlands wants a piece of the blockbuster pie

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

It's not a big deal outside of Asia, and I can't tell if article authors are unaware or chasing what they believe is the next giagantic game because the game China driving the huge numbers and everyone else seems to be rather average on it.

Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Clipfarming, influencer screenings, and meme-bait popcorn buckets: promoting a movie in the internet age is often a full-court offensive to get noticed. In that spirit, why not just get down to business and resort to modern civilization’s oldest method for seeking attention: dangling some money in people’s faces?

That’s what the marketing teams behind Amazon MGM Studios‘ “How to Rob a Bank” and Skydance’s “Ebenezer” have tried in the weeks leading up to their shared November 13 release to North American theaters.

For the former ensemble heist thriller, a branded ATM was moved between multiplexes throughout the Los Angeles area over the course of four days. Those who learned of the campaign on the film‘s social media channels could gain clues about the machine’s location and a specified PIN number, which would spark payouts of a single one-hundred-dollar bill to those who bothered to seek out (or stumble upon) it. Related Stories What Are Local Movie Theaters Showing on Election Night? Don’t Forget, Oscar Watchers: ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Project Hail Mary,’ and Other Big Guns Are Coming Back

“Ebenezer” took a more cheeky, trifling approach, promoting an official Venmo account for Johnny Depp’s Christmas crab apple that users could request funds from. Those who scrolled through the account’s transactions would see it shares the character’s penny-pinching spirit: the only completed transactions were those giving away one single cent. The Venmo account was only active for a few hours, though a Paramount Instagram post from last week teases followers to “check back” as “Ebenezer might be feeling generous on @venmo again.”

Several film news aggregation accounts like Culture Crave and DiscussingFilm reported that the account “crashed” due an overwhelming amount of requests, though Paramount declined to comment on if such a description was accurate. Venmo did not respond to a request asking if the company partnered with the studio on the sponsorship.

Much like that line, there is also a tackiness du jour to both money-mindset stunts, especially in a world where awards shows, professional sports and geopolitical events can hardly be watched without outlets asking you to bet — erh, predict — on them. A video posted to Paramount’s socials opens with a Venmo request for $500, asking Scrooge to help pay off a user’s student loans.

Not to mention the real inadvertent quirk: the account has been able to receive payments from users. Considering the scant number of one-cent payouts from the account and the number of influxes, it is almost certain that Paramount could have made money on the stunt, though an individual with knowledge of the account shared that all received funds were sent back to users via private transactions.

Krystyna Ursta, a 27-year-old actress, video editor, and Depp fan in Los Angeles, shared that she gave about $30 to the account and received a full refund a few days later — plus an extra penny and an invitation to a special screening of the film in New York on Monday. She will be attending a local press screening instead. Ursta also posted a video of herself reacting to the account, one of many fan responses that flooded in on social media.

“I kind of figured that they will probably return it,” Ursta wrote over text after being reached through her Instagram handle, which she included in her Venmo transactions. “I’m such a big fan. I was happy to support the film.”

The rather gimmick-less gimmick of waving around money also helps capture the attention of people that aren’t necessarily interested in seeing the movie, but are going through the average modern experience of thinking about one’s financial situation. Aggregation accounts were quick to post graphics reporting on both stunts, with captions like “HOW TO ROB A BANK ATM’S ARE BEING SET UP AROUND LOS ANGELES AND GIVING PEOPLE FREE MONEY AND IT COULDN’T HAPPEN AT A BETTER TIME” and “EBENEZER SCROOGE WILL SEND YOU REAL MONEY ON VENMO BUT THERE’S A CATCH SWIPE FOR MORE.”

There’s also people like Scott, a 35-year-old based out of Atlanta that couldn’t help but engage with the “Ebenezer” Venmo account after seeing it on X. He sent a penny, then received one in return. (A disclaimer: six Venmo users were reached for interview about their Ebenezer experience by sending them $0.01 with this reporter’s contact information in the caption; Scott was the only response that timed out before publication.)

“Seeing Ebenezer is now on Venmo was too funny and stupid to not engage with,” he wrote over text. “There’s something very boring dystopia about it: the idea of a fictional character from a 200-year-old Christmas story being commercialized on Venmo just shows how dumb Hollywood can. … It’s like McDonald’s Monopoly: take our slop and we might give your money.”

Also helpful for the studios is how little dangling the potential of money actually costs. Sans staffing fees, producing the “Ebenezer” Venmo account and its activity used a sum less than the coins between the couch cushions on the Paramount lot. Per the “How to Rob a Bank” promo’s website, each location’s prize pool gave away ten one-hundred-dollar bills and twenty twenty-dollar-bills ($1,400 total), plus some theater-supplied prizes like gift cards. An employee at the Regal Sherman Oaks that worked on the day of the on-site promotion said the ATM seemed to deal out the rewards in a random order, as opposed to $100 dollar bills for the first finders. Amazon MGM declined to comment, while Stellar Agency Inc., which sponsored and administered the promotion, did not respond to a request.

Both had much smaller overheads than a “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t” promotion than ran in April 2025. To launch the magician threequel’s first trailer, Lionsgate reportedly gave away roughly $250,000 to those that texted a mysterious phone number displaying in Times Square in the hours up to the drop. Like “Ebenezer” and “How to Rob a Bank,” it was a promotion that sparked a viral moment with plenty of user-generated content, each sharing the widely desired fantasy of receiving free money.

Neon handed out basic resources for an “I Love Boosters” promotion in May, where stars KeKe Palmer and LaKeith Stanfield took over a Shell gas station in West Pico to give out complimentary refills to the first 70 cars that arrived. The stunt played on then-peaking fuel prices, which had skyrocketed in the wake of the U.S.’ initial bombing of Iran in February and the subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

In the months since, President Trump has promised $5,000 checks to every adult U.S. citizen if the Republican Party retains control of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump announced the idea, his approval rating was at a dismal 35 percent, per a CNN aggregate of various polls. Though the offer is unprecedented and dubious on its face, it has been covered extensively — and it cost nothing to float it.

The 12 Years a Slave star was diagnosed with uterine fibroids—non-cancerous growths that develop in or around the uterus—in 2014, the same year she won an Oscar for performance in the movie.

However, it wasn't until 2025 when she disclosed her diagnosis, writing on Instagram that she had been "suffering in silence" for more than a decade.

"When we reach puberty, we're taught periods mean pain, and that pain is simply part of being a woman," she shared. "We're struggling alone with something that affects us most."

The Beverly Hills, 90210 alum revealed in April 2025 that he was recovering from surgery after his appendix nearly burst.

“Last week, I started feeling some pain in my stomach,” Brian said in an Instagram video at the time. “I ended up going to the emergency room, and I had a perforated appendix. Not quite burst, but just before.”

He added, “I'm on the road to recovery. It's not an easy process. This is my first major surgery.”

In July 2025, the Daisy Jones & The Six star shared that she had been hospitalized due to a hernia—a gap in the muscular wall that's commonly found in the abdomen or groin area—caused by wearing tight pants.

"'Suki you never tweet anymore,'" she wrote on X, formerly known as Twitter. "Have you ever considered I wore pants so tight 6 months ago it caused a hernia & I’ve been too scared to tell you?"

Savannah DeMelo's Mid-Game "Medical Emergency" Mid-Game

The Racing Louisville midfielder collapsed just a few minutes into her soccer team's September 2025 match against Seattle Reign at Lumen Field in Seatle.

The United States Women’s National Team player could be seen slowly sitting down on the field with a teammate by her side, per Reuters, as the referee called for trainers to check her out. She collapsed seconds later.

“Savannah received immediate on-field care from medical personnel and was transported to a local hospital for further evaluation,” the National Women’s Soccer League wrote on X later that night. “She is stable and alert."

Adam Devine's Long-Term Injury From Childhood Accident

Adam Devine shared that injuries he sustained after getting hit by a cement truck when he was 11 years old are still affecting him to this day.

“It’s been a nightmare,” Devine said in a 2025 episode of the In Depth With Graham Bensinger podcast. “I have spasms all over. For a while, [the doctors] told me I was dying—literally, within this last year.”

He noted that pain comes and goes, adding, "My body has all these things that are a little wonky and a little wrong with it."

The Bachelor Nation alum shared that he went to the hospital “crawling on all fours” due to overwhelming back pain that was aggravated during an RV trip with a friend.

“Right now, knees to my toes, it’s, like, still tingly, which is crazy,” he said on a March 2025 episode of his Trading Secrets podcast. “And to put in perspective, I don’t know, man, like not to sound douchey, but like two, three weeks ago, maybe a month ago, I was squatting probably like 295 pounds. And right now, I can’t do a squat on my foot. I can’t do a one legged squat, I fall. It’s like I had a stroke or something.”

But with the help of a back specialist and some steroids, he added, “We’re on the mend.”

Real Housewives of Orange County’s Gina Kirschenheiter shared her ex-husband Matt Kirschenheiter suffered a heart attack in March 2025, but thankfully survived the ordeal.

The 30 Rock star suffered a health scare at a New York Knicks basketball game in March 2025, leading to him being wheeled out of Madison Square Garden.

However, the comedian shared an update on social media the following day, noting it was a case of food poisoning and that he was on the mend.

The Even Stevens alum shared in February 2025 that she was shot in the face while on a trip to shoot clay pigeons to celebrate husband Brendan Rooney's birthday.

"There was another party with us and they unsafely fired in the wrong direction and shot me in the face," she wrote on Instagram. "@thebrendanrooney immediately sprung into action, assessed me, and rushed me to the hospital. I was hit in 5 places, one was less than an inch from hitting me directly in my right eye."

The Kim Possible alum continued, "Unfortunately a fragment got lodged behind my eye and it is too risky to remove surgically at this time. Doctors will continue to monitor me (I can see normally at the moment)."

The actress said she was grateful to be alive. "I love my daughters, husband, family, and friends so much," she said. "I saw my life flash before my eyes and I’m telling you, hug the people around you every chance you can. Life can change in an instant."

While the internet isn't always a kind place, Amy Schumer is happy that, in this case, it helped her get answers."The internet really came for me after doing a bunch of press, and I was like, 'OK everybody, relax,'" Amy recalled of her "puffier" face on a January 2025 episode of Call Her Daddy. "But then doctors were chiming in in the comments and they were like, 'No no, we think something’s really up. Your face looks so crazy that we think something’s up. And I’m like, ‘Wait, I’m getting trolled by doctors?’"After these doctors said they thought she had Cushing syndrome and that it may be caused by spiking coritsol levels or steroid injections, the Life & Beth creator thought, "Wait, I have been getting steroid injections in my scars.""I had a breast reduction, a C-section, whatever, and so I was getting these steroid injections," Amy said. "So it gave me this thing called Cushing syndrome, which I wouldn’t have known if the internet hadn’t come for me so hard."Toda, Amy is just relieved she's OK. As she shared in a February 2024 News Not Noise newsletter, "Finding out I have the kind of Cushing that will just work itself out and I'm healthy was the greatest news imaginable."

Casey Fitzgerald's Neck Injury From Hockey Skate Blade

The AHL player was cut by a fellow player's skate during a game in December 2024 and received 25 stitches. His father, New Jersey Devils general manager Tom Fitzgerald later told ESPN after his son was fully recovered, "We're very lucky. I don't wish that on any parent."

Hailey Bieber had the "scariest moment" of her life when she was having breakfast with husband Justin Bieber and started experiencing stroke-like symptoms in March 2022."Justin was like, 'Are you OK?'" the Rhode skincare mogul shared a month later on YouTube, "and I just didn't respond because I wasn't sure. And then he asked me again and when I went to respond, I couldn't speak. The right side of my face started drooping. I couldn't get a sentence out."While Hailey said the facial drooping stopped and her speech came back, she went to the hospital to make sure she was OK."They did some scans and they were able to see that I had suffered a small blood clot to my brain," the model added, "which they labeled and categorized as something called a TIA [Transient Ischemic Attack]."Later, Hailey went to the University of California, Los Angeles, where she found out she had a hole in her heart called a patent foramen ovale (PFO).She explained the blood clot had traveled into her heart, "escaped" through the hole and went to her brain, leading to the TIA.Hailey said she had a successful PFO closure procedure and was now feeling great.

The same year Hailey had her health scare, Justin experienced one of his own.In June 2022, the "Baby" singer shared he was diagnosed with Ramsay Hunt syndrome, a condition that caused temporary paralysis to parts of his face and forced him to cancel the remainder of his Justice World Tour."It is from this virus that attacks the nerve in my ear and my facial nerves and has caused my face to have paralysis," Justin explained in an Instagram video at the time. "As you can see, this eye is not blinking. I can't smile on this side of my face. This nostril will not move. So, there's full paralysis on this side of my face."In fact, he told his followers it had gotten "progressively harder to eat." But after a while, the paralysis went away."He's doing really well," Hailey said on a June 2022 episode of Good Morning America, later adding, "He's feeling a lot better. Obviously, it was just a very scary and random situation to happen, but he's going to be totally OK and I'm just grateful that he's fine."

While Jamie Foxx initially kept details of his April 2023 hospitalization private, he later opened up about what he went through.One day in Atlanta, "I was having such a bad headache, so I asked my boy, I said, ‘Listen, I need an aspirin,’” the Oscar winner said in his 2024 Netflix special What Had Happened Was... “Before I could get the Aspirin, I went out. I don’t remember 20 days.”Jamie said he was initially taken to a doctor who gave him a cortisone shot and then sent him home. However, his concerned sister Deidra Dixon then drove him to a hospital, where they got an answer: He had a brain bleed that led to a stroke.Twenty days after undergoing an operation, the Django Unchained woke up May 4 in a wheelchair and couldn’t walk. He then went to Chicago for rehabilitation and therapy."All I can tell you is that I appreciate every prayer,” he said, “because I needed every prayer.”

Tracey Yukich's Medical Emergency on The Biggest Loser

The reality star revealed that she "died" while running a mile during the first challenge of the NBC competition series.

“I don't remember a lot,” she explained on Fit for TV: The Reality of The Biggest Loser. “I remember hearing the helicopter. I just felt like I was floating. And then my grandpa was there. And then I saw darkness. But then I saw light. So I knew, I knew I died that day.”

“My organs were literally shutting down,” she continued. “I didn't realize that I had rhabdomyolysis. And rhabdomyolysis is your body's way of saying, ‘I'm going to shut down on you.’”

Emilia Clarke filmed battle scenes for Game of Thrones, but in 2019, she published an essay in The New Yorker titled "A Battle for My Life."Having a bad headache at the gym, "I reached the toilet, sank to my knees, and proceeded to be violently, voluminously ill," the actress wrote. "Meanwhile, the pain—shooting, stabbing, constricting pain—was getting worse. At some level, I knew what was happening: my brain was damaged."She was taken to the hospital for a brain scan."The diagnosis was quick and ominous: a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), a life-threatening type of stroke, caused by bleeding into the space surrounding the brain," the Emmy nominee added. "I’d had an aneurysm, an arterial rupture."Emilia had immediate surgery to seal the aneurysm, calling the pain "unbearable." While she was recovering, she continued, she experienced aphasia and was "muttering nonsense."A week later, "the aphasia passed," Emilia added, and she left the hospital a month after being admitted. At a 2013 brain scan, she learned a growth "doubled in size" and that she needed surgery again."When they woke me, I was screaming in pain," she wrote. "The procedure had failed. I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "Everybody just came to my rescue."Because of other medical concerns, Cori ended up staying in the hospital longer than she initially expected."I could have went home after my stroke, but my lupus wasn't doing so well," the Snoop's Fatherhood: Cori and Wayne's Story star continued. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

Shailene Woodley’s early 20s were not an easy time health-wise.“It got to the point where I was losing my hearing. I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

Amazon rewrites its software engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

by Todd Bishop on Nov 3, 2026 at 12:26 pmNovember 3, 2026 at 12:36 pm

Last month, a small team inside Amazon Web Services called Velocity Labs went from concept to the public release of a new open-source AI model in less than a week.

The group, whose existence hasn’t been previously reported, was formed in April. Velocity Labs has about 35 people, most of them in Seattle. The idea is to think beyond Amazon’s normal product-oriented approach, building quick prototypes in areas of AI that the company sees as underexplored and increasingly important to customers.

“We have noticed how the open-source community, and some of our competitors, experiment with new ideas, and deliver initial products fast,” the company says in job listings. “With Velocity Labs we are building an organization that can move faster, explore more, and make sure AWS is at the cutting edge of innovation in agentic AI.”

Inside the group, scientists and engineers work together, and they’re encouraged to cross over: engineers engage in research, and scientists do engineering work.

Velocity Labs is an example of the ways Amazon is trying “to create organizations that we think are going to be better suited to working with this new set of tools,” said Marc Brooker, an AWS vice president and distinguished engineer who leads the team.

For the vast majority of Amazon’s developers, he said, AI agents now write almost all the code that would have previously been written by hand.

Redefining the role: The team is part of Amazon’s larger rethinking of software development for the AI era, laid out in revised guidelines that the company’s engineering leaders sent to its developers earlier this year.

A letter that accompanied the guidelines, published last week under the byline of Michael “Terk” Terkowitz, a VP and distinguished engineer in Amazon’s stores business, advises engineers to learn AI now and to stay close to their customers and products.

The letter acknowledges that as Amazon has grown, some engineers and managers have become “less connected to their customers and business.”

Amazon has never published its underlying role guidelines for software engineers, and it declined to provide a copy of the revised version for this article. Brooker, one of the authors of the accompanying letter, said in an interview that the update emphasizes measuring engineers and teams by outcomes rather than inputs.

“We had seen these anti-patterns in the industry of folks really focusing on how many tokens are you spending, how many lines of code are you committing,” Brooker said, explaining that those kinds of measures don’t equate to customer value.

Asked whether AI use is part of performance reviews or promotions, Brooker said, “Not directly in a metrics sense.” It could factor in, he said, to the extent that it makes someone a stronger performer.

The letter doesn’t dismiss usage metrics entirely. Amazon has found that they “correlate well with the outputs that matter” and expects that to continue “for some time,” it says.

But what’s important, the letter says, is to use them “with care and judgement.”

Amazon engineers have described pressure to use AI tools. Three developers told The New York Times last year that managers were pushing them to use AI, raising output goals and becoming less forgiving about deadlines, with some coders saying their jobs had begun to resemble warehouse work. Amazon has set a goal for more than 80% of its developers to use AI each week, the Financial Times reported.

In May, Amazon shut down an internal leaderboard called KiroRank — which ranked employees by how much they used Kiro, the company’s AI coding tool — after finding that some were using the tool excessively just to climb the rankings, the FT reported.

Asked whether that episode was part of the impetus for the revised guidelines, Brooker said he didn’t recall the leaderboard or the details surrounding it.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.”

Letter accompanying the revised SDE role guidelines

How the work has changed: Two years ago, most Amazon developers were still writing their code by hand, Brooker said. Today, “for the vast majority of our developer population, almost all of their implementation code is agent generated rather than human written,” he said.

“That is a massive change in the way of working for software engineers,” he said.

Brooker said he used to spend much of his time in a traditional code editor or the command line, and now spends a lot more of it working with agent tools such as Kiro, Kiro Crew and Anthropic’s Claude Code, calling it “a complete change of tools.”

For the company, the transition hasn’t been seamless. In March, Amazon acknowledged that an engineer who followed inaccurate advice from an AI agent contributed to one of several outages on its retail site, though the company disputed a Financial Times report that junior and mid-level engineers would need senior engineers to sign off on AI-assisted changes.

Amazon also pushed back on an earlier FT report that a 13-hour disruption to an AWS service in December happened after engineers let its Kiro AI coding tool make changes, and the tool decided to “delete and recreate the environment.” Amazon blamed user error — a misconfigured role — and said it has since added safeguards, including mandatory peer review for production access.

Still, the letter acknowledges that today’s AI tools won’t help in every situation, and it says that’s OK as long as engineers can explain why.

“If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing,” the letter says. “An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for.”

Inside Velocity Labs: The group is part of the agentic AI division led by Swami Sivasubramanian, which has organized much of its work around small teams of six to eight people, as GeekWire reported in June. Velocity Labs also includes the developers behind Strands, AWS’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents.

The model that Velocity Labs released last month, Strands Decider 2B, is designed to make quick, narrow decisions inside AI agents, such as which tool to use or where to route a request. It’s based on Qwen, an open model from Alibaba, and was released Oct. 1 along with the recipe used to train it.

Brooker built the original version on his own GPU at home after the startup TypeSafe AI unveiled Jev, a similar decision model, on Sept. 15, he wrote on his blog. “Every line of code was written by an agent,” he wrote, though he tried to make sure “the core ideas and insights were mine, or at least I understood them.”

Brooker described the team’s turnaround as less than a week from concept to public release. OpenAI announced a similar hosted service, its Decisions API, the same week, TechCrunch reported.

Brooker credited the team’s speed to its small size and a high level of trust: each person takes ownership of a piece of a project and asks for help when needed. He expects Amazon to create more teams like it, though not across the whole company.

Impact on jobs: Amazon has cut roughly 30,000 corporate jobs since late 2025. CEO Andy Jassy has said he expects AI to shrink the company’s corporate workforce over time.

At the same time, AWS CEO Matt Garman said in April that Amazon is “hiring just as many software developers as we ever had,” Business Insider reported. An Amazon spokesperson told the publication that more than 11,000 interns and early-career software engineers would join the company globally this year.

Asked whether AI will mean fewer engineers at Amazon, Brooker said, “I don’t think it changes the number of engineers.” The company wants engineers who take ownership, are curious and can learn quickly outside their areas of expertise, he said.

AI isn’t the right answer for every problem, Brooker said.

If the right tool is “an AI agent powered by a cutting-edge model, fantastic,” he said. However, he added, if it’s “three lines of Python code, that’s great too.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

The Six Wild Campaign Ads Definitely Not Destined for the Paley Center

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

As the election season comes to a merciful close, maybe the real treasure is the absurd spots we met along the way.

There are many things the country can’t agree on, as will be evident when results for a series of close Congressional races begin rolling in Tuesday night.But there is one thing we can agree on: the campaign ads need to stop. They are everywhere, like ants at a picnic, or aunts in a political WhatsApp chat. And they need to go.On Wednesday they will, but not before putting a big dent in our collective psyche. Republicans and Democrats combined to spend $11.6 billion on campaign ads, a record-breaking sum for any cycle. (Elon Musk himself spent nearly half a billion dollars on GOP candidates, which may or may not turn out to be a better investment than the $1 billion SpaceX spent on Skydance to maybe not distribute a documentary.) Imagine if that $11.6 billion was spent on, like, going to the movies. Actually, that figure is literally $3 billion more than Americans shelled out at the box office last year and on par with the all-time $11 billion-plus highs of the late 2010s.Of course all that money led to studios producing some pretty cool movies. Did this cash yield any meaningful cultural output? Is there some hidden masterpiece, some Madison Avenue Black Panther, to show for all the outlays?Well, not exactly. But we do have Obama shooting hoops in a gym, a senior citizen shooting an intruder in her home and Steve Hilton going softcore. Here are the six wild anti-classics this cycle yielded, and what you might have missed if you weren’t in these localities/was watching anything more sane including a Jets game.—1. Shooting Cranks

“Four score and seven years ago.” Ask not what your country can you do for you.” “You break into my house, you’re gonna get shot.” The North Carolina state legislator Jennifer Balkcom wasn’t terribly well-known before this election cycle. Then she ran for the competitive House seat in a district centered on Asheville in the western part of the state. And thanks to going full Lowry Gang, and her mother going full Ma Barker, we now can’t not know her. Apparently Balkcom’s nice white-haired mom was home once, someone broke in, and she shot the intruder, as a smiling and nodding Jennifer recalls sitting next to her storytelling mother over a kitchen-table cup of coffee. “Mom’s a fighter,” Balkcom smiles and shrugs. We’re not sure why any of this would be a reason to vote for her, but it does make you rethink that family vacation to the Blue Ridge Mountains.

2. Don’t Even Ask About The Lunch Special

Barack Obama was on the campaign trail a lot this season, but perhaps his most notable stop was in an Iowa gym with Democratic Senate candidate (and former Paralympian Gold medalist) Josh Turek to shoot hoops to support the candidate’s surprisingly viable challenge to turn the seat blue. You won’t learn much about the candidate’s policy views, but you will learn that Turek has perimeter game, that Mr. President still loves a good matchup of H-O-R-S-E (or, I-O-W-A) and where each of the two men ranks Kareem all time. (Obama has him higher.) They both put Jordan ahead of LeBron, an empirically wrong take, but otherwise this ad is pretty much harmless. The subtle message is that Turek is a doer, and that he hangs out with Obama. There are worse codes to transmit — the former president won the state handily in both 2008 and 2012, the last time a Democrat did.

Speaking of Iowa, is it particularly cinema-obsessed? Turek’s opponent Ashley Hinson did a whole number in a movie theater with an awkward “working across the aisle” metaphor,” in which she sits in a multiplex and hands popcorn and candy to an unseen denim-shirted hand reaching out creepily from another section (is this supposed to be indicative of what we do in a theater?) while talking about her allegedly bipartisan legislative efforts. She says, for instance, that she collaborated with local Democrats to expand benefits to veterans (this is challenged by Democrats) and that she also worked “with President Trump to take on health-insurance companies to lower your costs.” What such work entails is unclear; the closest that can be surmised is that Hinson supported Trump’s notorious Medicaid cuts as well his notion of moving ACA tax credits into an HSA account — an idea often discredited for putting millions into debt. Neither of which one might be expected to brag about. The ad ends with someone spilling popcorn in Hinson’s lap as they’re trying to get to their seat, which seems metaphoric, or at least a lot more indicative of what actually happens in a movie theater.

5. At Least It Was Good Product Placement?Back in 2012, in an incident you might want to Google, Ken Paxton was entering a Dallas-area courthouse when he spied a $1,000 Montblanc pen that had been left behind the security tray by an attorney named Joe Joplin entering the courthouse, prompting Paxton to rummage around and quietly put it in his pocket, with surveillance footage capturing the whole episode. Michael Haneke himself could not dream up this scenario. Anyway, the incident has rightly dogged Paxton on the campaign trail ever since, and it surfaced again this cycle in a James Talarico ad (part of a record-breaking $600 million Texas-race spend), with the Talarico campaign going so far as to actually track down Joplin and put him on camera to endorse the candidate. The ad asks: “Ken Paxton steals pens. What will he steal from you?” Not sure. But at least he gave us this cultural treasure.

6. He’s Never Done Anything Like This BeforeSteve Hilton has proved to be one of the more entertaining figures on the campaign trail this season. The British-born, Silicon Valley-dwelling former Fox News host has made full use of his scrapper political past — there’s a reason he inspired a character in Armando Iannucci’s satire The Thick of It. Nowhere was that more evident than this (possibly AI-generated) spot. A softly lit Skinemax-esque tableau featuring two young women in bed accompanying a double entendre-y “Just Try It” message all hinting at sapphic experimentation but really voting Republican in California is so unbelievably obvious and low-aiming it almost works. Not sure the “Now lick it” double-entendre at the end will win any subtlety awards (it was the mail-in ballot). But Hilton did prove an important point: when you have no chance of winning, go for the most shameless and laugh-inducing form of virality. Hilton is extremely unlikely to win, but he did move the needle by proposing an eye-popping 60 percent tax credit. Thanks to this ad, we now know the kind of mise-en-scene it might have been used for.
