The Strait of Hormuz closure has cost Europe an extra $142 billion for the same energy it was already buying

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Four years after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine forced Europe to scramble for new energy suppliers, the bloc is in another fuel crisis. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said this week Europe has paid an extra €127 billion (a little over $142 billion) for imported oil and gas since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and it has received no additional energy in return for it.

“Since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, imported fossil fuels cost Europe an additional €127 billion without a single molecule of energy in addition,” von der Leyen said in a keynote at the WinWin Brussels Summit.

In April, about seven weeks into the war, the Commission put the extra cost at €24 billion (about $27 billion). By late September, EU energy commissioner Dan Jørgensen said it had passed €100 billion (about $111 billion), similarly echoing our ninth-grade science class building and saying that the bloc hadn’t received “one extra molecule of gas or oil.”

“When we import oil and gas, we risk importing the shocks and crises that come with them,” von der Leyen said at the keynote.

After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Moscow cut gas flows to the EU to a trickle, and governments scrambled to fill storage at record prices, with the bloc eventually vowing to wean itself off Russian energy. As a result, Russia’s share of EU gas imports fell from about 45% before the invasion to about 13% in 2025. In January, EU members adopted a ban ending Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports by the end of this year and pipeline gas by autumn 2027.

But Europe largely replaced Russian gas with other imports, much of it LNG shipped from the U.S. and the Middle East. When the Iran war began, the EU still got 57% of its energy from imported fossil fuels.

The war then shut the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway that carried about one-fifth of the world’s traded oil. Tanker traffic through the strait nearly stopped. After a cold winter, EU gas storage stood at just 28.4% in late March, below the five-year average. The Persian Gulf also supplied more than 40% of Europe’s jet fuel and diesel imports.

Within weeks, Jørgensen asked member states to consider “voluntary demand-saving measures”, especially in transport. The International Energy Agency’s plan to cut oil use included car-free Sundays, a rationing tactic from the 1970s oil crisis.

By September, drivers in some EU countries were paying nearly 50% more at the pump, or more than $11 a gallon. In Italy, a weeklong truckers’ strike over diesel prices halted deliveries of milk to mozzarella makers, and as Italian inflation hit 5.4%. EU officials expect oil and gas prices to stay above prewar levels until at least the end of 2027.

The IEA said Tuesday the EU gas storage is entering the heating season at its lowest level since 2013, warning that in a cold winter with continued Hormuz disruptions, storage could fall below 10% by the end of March. EU gas network operators have warned of a shortfall of 12% to 15% of demand in a severe cold snap, and energy ministers met in late October to discuss EU-wide limits on consumption.

While Vladimir Putin said in March Russia was ready to supply Europe again, Von der Leyen called a return to Russian fuel a “strategic blunder.”

On Tuesday, she argued Europe’s answer is to import less.

“This year, we have again seen the devastating impact of climate change. Droughts, wildfires, floods,” she said. “But we have also seen the cost of our dependence on imported fossil fuels.”

The EU has pledged to become climate-neutral by 2050 and to cut emissions 90% by 2040. Von der Leyen said more than €1.2 trillion has been invested in sustainable activities across the bloc since 2021.

“So let me be crystal clear: Europe will stay the course, we stick to our targets, and we back our clean industries,” she said.

Catherina covers markets, the economy, energy, tech, and AI.

WoW: Forever Shamans Are Protesting Class Changes After Being “Completely Ignored”

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

World of Warcraft: Forever just received a massive batch of class-balance updates ahead of launch that have boosted power across the board, but one group of players isn't happy with the changes: Shamans.

Developer Blizzard recently released Forever's launch patch notes based on feedback and data accumulated during the beta, resulting in a power spike for all classes and major reworks for classes like Paladin and Rogue. Shamans, too, received some significant changes, most notably the removal of a key Elemental specialization ability, Lava Burst, along with any interactions other abilities had with it.

It's that change, and other changes to specialization-specific abilities like Restoration's Riptide and Enhancement's Maelstrom Weapon, that have resulted in the WoW Classic Shaman Discord going into lockdown in protest. The entire server, which has around 80,000 members, has been made read-only, with a message declaring the reason for why it took what it described as such a "drastic measure."

"Community feedback gets completely ignored and class fantasies are getting destroyed," the server declared. "With this we intend to give them [Blizzard] a sign and show them that the community is not [happy] with how they approached our beloved class. Give us back our class and spec identities and fantasies."

While the protest is in regards to class changes in Forever specifically, the server is also home to Shaman discussions as they relate to other "classic" versions of the game as well, including WoW Classic and Mists of Pandaria Classic. As of writing, all of those channels are also locked and set to read-only. 

In a follow-up post, the server went into more detail about its complaints in regards to how Blizzard has approached Forever's Shaman design. It stated its complaints aren't about "damage output." It also made clear the server will re-open "regardless of the outcome," but that it felt like its feedback through "legitimate" channels were being ignored. 

The server then proceeded to list what it viewed as wrong with various ability changes for each Shaman specialization. It additionally called attention to what it called the "hybrid spell power issue," where spell power and intellect gear seems to be better for not only Elemental but also Enhancement, muddying the identity between the two specializations. 

Blizzard has previously said it doesn't want "hybrid" classes that can deal damage and heal, like Shamans, to deal more damage than dedicated DPS classes. Players in the WoW community refer to this idea as the "hybrid tax," something those running the Shaman Discord said they are fine with if it means Shaman class design is improved.

"Truthfully, hybrid tax us all you want if the result is a cohesive class with strong class fantasy elements that are actually represented in our playstyles," it said. 

This isn't the first time a WoW class Discord shut down in protest of how class changes. As pointed out by Wowhead, back in August 2025, the modern WoW Paladin Discord was partially closed in protest of the Retribution specialization's raid performance. In that case, only Retribution-specific channels were locked, and the entire protest lasted less than 24 hours. Blizzard did announce Retribution Paladin buffs shortly after, though it's unclear if those changes came at least in part due to the server protest or not.

How long the WoW Classic Shaman Discord remains in lockdown remains to be seen, but Forever launches November 4. Blizzard recently said it doesn't expect to make any more major class changes for at least another month.

UK AI minister says a serious cyber breach is ‘extremely likely’

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Kanishka Narayan says government bodies and companies are underprepared as AI tools make hacking faster.

Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s minister for artificial intelligence.

UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan said a serious cyber breach is “extremely likely” in both the public and private sector, and that neither is ready. He pointed to extra funding for the AI Security Institute as the government’s response.

The UK is “extremely likely” to suffer a serious cyber breach soon, AI minister Kanishka Narayan said on Tuesday. Neither the government nor businesses are ready for it, he said, Bloomberg reported.

“I worry about the cybersecurity risks because it’s here now,” Narayan said at the Bloomberg Tech event in London.

“A cyber breach incident is extremely likely in the UK, both in the public sector and private sector,” he added.

His warning came hours after Richard Horne, head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, said British firms were “willfully blind” to threats from Russia, Iran and China. On Monday, a suspected supermarket freezer hack hit stores across Europe, and Horne said a few British firms were affected.

AI is adding to the worry. Hackers are thought to be using AI tools to speed up attacks. This summer, AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others broke out of test environments and breached outside websites.

Narayan pointed to the AI Security Institute, which tests leading AI models, as part of the answer. The government gave it an extra £120M in its latest budget. Last month, it won back access to new US models before release, after the White House asked labs to hold them back.

Narayan would not say how long that access would last. “Nothing is a particular guarantee in the world of AI,” he said.

I reviewed the new iPad mini: It’s the best Apple tablet, with a price to match

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Key specs: 8.5-inch OLED display, A20 Pro chip, and just 5.4mm thin

What we loved: Incredible, lightweight design, strong performance, and a beautiful display

What we didn't love: The $699 starting price

The new iPad Mini is here — I'm looking right at its super-bright OLED display as I type this review — and it's beautiful. The lightest Apple tablet ever made, the iPad Mini has the same powerhouse A20 Pro chip as the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and even though it may not be the ideal device for intensive work, it can still support local AI workloads, not to mention the new Siri AI.

But why oh why does everything have to be so damn expensive in 2026? That's not a serious question — we know exactly who's hogging all the RAM, and putting Apple under pressure from memory makers. But for folks like me who have to count every dollar, the starting $699 price does hurt.

So, as much as I loved using the new iPad Mini (it really is a lot of fun), I'm not quite sure who to recommend this device to, unless you're in the top income tax bracket.

Let's cut to the chase: The iPad Mini is now my favorite tablet in the Apple lineup. It has an incredible display, excellent design, and strong performance. However, I'm not quite sure who should buy it.

I'm not the only reviewer who's a little confused by Apple's product lineup in 2026. At first, I thought the iPad Mini was the MacBook Neo of the iPad family. It's the smaller, less powerful model for everyday use. That makes intuitive sense, but it's also wrong.

The iPad Mini offers better performance in many respects than the iPad Air and a far superior display. And while the MacBook Neo is a budget laptop, the iPad Mini is definitely not a budget device. Its starting price is only $50 less than the iPad Air.

A slightly cheaper iPad Mini priced around $499 or $599 would make a lot more sense to me, and be much easier to recommend.

After testing the device, I can heartily recommend the iPad Mini to one-percenters looking for the best iPad for everyday use. But you can also get Amazon's new Alexa Pro tablets, and plenty of other good tablets, for well under $500, and most people will be perfectly fine without an OLED display or a chip that supports local AI models.

Given all that, I'm just not sure I'd pay $699 for the iPad Mini. Plus, the model I tested, which came with 512GB, the Nano-texture display, and the C2 cellular chip, would have set me back $1,249, almost twice as much — and that's definitely not in my budget.

Now, most people can skip the cellular and stick with WiFi only. The Nano-texture finish is also non-essential. And if you rely on iCloud, you can make do with 128GB of storage, bringing the price back down to $699. But that's still a big ask.

I praised the M4 iPad Air for its excellent design, but the new iPad Mini is somehow even thinner. I also found its more compact size to be pretty much perfect for streaming, browsing, gaming, and scrolling. It fits just right in your hands.

Apple made some other design changes as well. The new iPad Mini no longer has speaker holes at the bottom of the device, which will inevitably get filled up with gunk and lint. Instead, sound emanates from the device as part of a new Acoustic Display technology. And because the device is fully enclosed, it achieves IP67 water and dust resistance for extra durability. I haven't dunked my iPad Mini in the bathtub (yet), but it should withstand brief immersion in water.

I'm used to the larger iPad Air, and I instantly preferred the smaller, lighter design of the iPad Mini. I can see why the device has such devoted fans in the Apple community.

One design note: Apple moved the microphone and 12MP Center Stage camera to the side bezel of the device. Because I'm not used to it, I kept thinking it was a bit of schmutz on the screen and kept trying to wipe it off with my thumb. I got used to it, and so will you.

My only complaint about the design? It has Touch ID instead of Face ID.

Apple upgraded the iPad Mini with an OLED display, and it's fantastic. The clarity is so precise, and the brightness, color clarity, and deep blacks are instantly noticeable, especially when watching HDR content (the iPad Mini has a peak brightness of 1,200 nits with HDR).

I used the iPad Mini side by side with the iPad Air while watching my go-to monitor-testing video, and the difference was clear. The blacks are jet-black, the colors jump off the screen, and even the smallest details are so sharp. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Now, I have to call out that the iPad Mini display doesn't rise to the level of the iPad Pro.

The tandem OLED display on the latest M5 iPad Pro remains unrivaled in the tablet world. It's so good that the iPad Pro can act as a reference monitor for film editors, which is not something you can say about the Mini. The iPad Mini also lacks the ProMotion tech that gives the Pro its high, smooth refresh rate.

But these are minor quibbles that almost no one outside the tech or video-editing world really needs to care about.

To recap: The iPad Mini's OLED display absolutely rules.

I wouldn't call the Nano-texture finish (which adds $200 to the price) a must-have, but it is pretty phenomenal. It's also available on the iPad Pro and the new iPhone Duo, and it virtually eliminates reflections and glare thanks to microscopic glass-etching technology that's hard to wrap your head around.

Even when I shone a bright flashlight directly at the display, you could barely see it. And with the OLED and nano-texture combined, you can watch content even in direct sunlight. It's like a magic trick.

Instead of using a past-gen chip, the new iPad Mini gets the same super-powered chip as the new iPhone 18 Pro Max and iPhone Duo. And it's a damn fine chip. I put the iPad Mini through the Geekbench 7 benchmarking test, and it compares favorably to the iPad Air and iPad Pro, coming somewhere between the M4 chip in the latest iPad Air and the M5 chip in the iPad Pro.

Here are the single- and multi-core Geekbench 7 scores for each of Apple's tablets. (Note: I ran Geekbench 7 on the Mini and Air myself and used Geekbench's average for the 11-inch M5 iPad Pro.)

What does this mean for the average user? Single-core scores are a good measure of overall "zippiness" for everyday use, according to Mashable laptop reviewer Haley Henschel, while the multi-core score is a better measure of overall performance for complex, longer-running tasks.

The scores indicate that the iPad Mini can support multitasking as well as a laptop, which matches my experience. I made sure not to close any apps while testing the Mini, and it never slowed down. The A20 Pro chip can also support Apple Intelligence features such as visual intelligence and photo editing, as well as run powerful local models.

That being said, I'm not sure many people will be working much on the iPad Mini. If you're doing complex video editing, engineering, or photo retouching, the larger displays on the iPad Air and Pro are better suited to these tasks. The iPad Mini doesn't even support Magic Keyboard.

The new Acoustic Display technology on the iPad Mini works really well, which isn't a surprise. Apple doesn't really release anything half-baked. The speakers were surprisingly good, and the new Mini has new tweeters and woofers for music and streaming. The audio does end up sounding a little tinny, but that's to be expected.

Taking pictures with an iPad is very boomer-coded, and the 12MP Center Stage cameras are better suited to quick selfies and video calls than to true photography. And for FaceTime purposes, the cameras get the job done.

Only you can decide if the $699 iPad Mini fits into your budget. Apple products are sometimes luxury items and status symbols, and that's becoming even more true in the age of RAMageddon and higher prices.

If price were no object, the iPad Mini would be an easy recommendation. Setting price aside for a minute, it puts competitors to shame and offers better design and display than the iPad Air.

As Politicians Break Promises, This Public Artwork Keeps Them

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Paul Ramírez Jonas debuted his participatory artwork “Public Trust” months before Trump was first elected. A decade on, it feels more urgent than ever.

Last month, Paul Ramírez Jonas invited the people of Toronto to sit down with a stranger in a public space, make a promise, swear on it, see it spelled out on a large-scale marquee, and then memorialize it in a one-of-a-kind contract they kept. One of hundreds of such vows was: “I promise to disagree better.”

Ramírez Jonas’s participatory public artwork “Public Trust,” presented by The Bentway (where Anna Gallagher-Ross directs programming), was commissioned and first showcased by Now + There (founded by Kate Gilbert and later renamed the Boston Public Art Triennial) in 2016, months before Donald Trump was elected as president.

“Public Trust” was the Now + There’s first project, a labor of love for its one-and-a-half-person team, and has since set the standard for its commissions. The promises made by everyday Bostonians — often similar in their commitments to family or self-improvement but coming from very different walks of life — were juxtaposed with daily headlines, including promises by politicians, corporations, weather forecasters, and more. This intermingling of commitments, both personal and authoritative, invites us to reflect on the power of our words, participation, and role in the democratic process. Ramírez Jonas often quips that he would like this project to one day become irrelevant.

Ten years later, in the lead-up to our municipal election in Toronto, we could think of no better project to invite people to reflect on the power of their words and their participation. Why does the simple act of sitting across from a stranger and making a promise feel more important than ever?

31 Moments That Made The Dragon Age Series Unforgettable

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

BioWare’s closure last month has put a lot of focus on the Mass Effect series, as the shutdown also coincided with the cancelation of the fifth game in the studio’s sci-fi series. But the company’s fantasy series,Â Dragon Age, also deserves some eulogizing. All fourÂ Dragon Age games are vastly different, spanning different RPG frameworks, fantasy subgenres, and corners of the world of Thedas. Though BioWare left some dangling threads at the end ofÂ Dragon Age: The Veilguard, it also seemed like the studio was focusing on narrative closure, just in case this was the last time anyone in the studio would get to go back to the universe it had created over four games and 15 years. With BioWare gone, let’s look back at some of the best moments from all four games.

Dragon Age: Origins begins with one of six playable opening chapters, the one you play based on the race and class of character you choose, providing a unique background for your character before they head out into the main story.

The Hero of Ferelden can be part of human nobility facing a tragic series of losses, a castless dwarf struggling to make it in the city of Orzamar, or a mage evicted from the magic school theyâve known their entire life, and those starkly different origin points are only half of the options. These origins define how your hero will be viewed in the dozens of hours that follow, and also function as a starting point for how a new player will view the franchise. I started as a Mage when I first played Dragon Age: Origins in 2009, and have always felt like a veteran of the Circle at heart. Future Dragon Age games would implement this concept of different player backgrounds with Inquisition and The Veilguard, but none would do it as thoroughlyâOrigins was the only time I got to see that history play out in real-time.

No character in Origins is as impactful as Morrigan, the enigmatic Witch of the Wilds. The apostate carries a sense of superiority toward the rest of the party, as well as the trials and tribulations of Thedas. When you meet her in the early hours of Origins, you still donât know much about the world, but her commanding presence elevated by Claudia Blackâs excellent voice performance tells you that she is unlike anyone or anything youâve met so far. Morrigan is one of the few characters in Dragon Age who watches nearly every important moment in Thedasâ history unfold, so seeing her here, both enigmatic but still so young and naive, is chilling to look back on.

After youâve picked your background and lived out whatever trauma is associated with it, Dragon Age: Origins puts you at the center of a battle with a darkspawn horde. Your job is to signal for reinforcements to help defeat an army of bloodthirsty monsters, but before the battle starts, the vibes seem off. The golden retriever King Cailain is jazzed about the incoming battle, though his father-in-law Loghain Mac Tir seems less enthusiastic. The tension between the two is tangible, but who are you to get involved in royal family affairs? However, when you signal for reinforcements, Loghain instead commands his forces to retreat, leaving everyone, including you and his own son-in-law, for dead at the hands of the Blight. Most of the preceding origin stories are full of some kind of betrayal. You might think you would get some respite from it at some point, but Origins doubles down, reminding you that you know nothing of this world and the lengths people will go to get what they want.

Origins is not an entirely grimdark fantasy dramaâsome of the best character interactions come from your party members hanging out with your dog companion. Though Mabari dogs are trained to be vicious combatants, your canine companion is a sweetheart. Many interactions between the party and dog give him a hard time for being a mangy mutt, only for him to be revealed as a sensitive soul who just wants to play. Examine your preconceived notions, Origins crew. The sharp fangs mask that the Mabari is actually a good boy.

There are several points in the Dragon Age series in which a party member can turn on you, but none have ever been quite as shocking as when the religious bard Leliana, and otherwise kind-hearted Wynne, turn on you if you taint the Urn of Sacred Ashes. This is a crime against one of the most prominent doctrines in all of Thedas, and bringing two of the most devout members of the party to watch is bound to cause drama, but Origins takes it a step further by having both of your teammates take up arms against you.

It doesnât matter how far youâve progressed through their personal stories, or even if youâre involved in a romance with Leliana; faith trumps all other emotions here, and you will have to strike down your allies. Youâll face plenty more betrayals during the Dragon Age series, but Leliana and Wynneâs heel turn is still one of the most sudden and violent.

Much like killing Leliana, Origins has a few choices whose ramifications were so earth-shattering that BioWare later had to write themselves out of the box theyâd created so they could re-use characters that could be dead. One of those was the option to kill Flemeth, Morriganâs even more enigmatic mother who allegedly wanted to steal her daughterâs body as a vessel to live longer, though the reality is a bit more nuanced than that. When Morrigan finds out about this plan, she begs you to slay the old woman in her hut in the woods. You can choose to do so or strike a deal with her to spare her in exchange for her grimoire of old spells, but choosing to slay her means fighting her in a powerful dragon form. Itâs a tough fight, but doing so leaves you not with a rewarding cutscene and major story revelation, but instead an unsettling and anticlimactic quiet. Youâre left with more mysteries than you had when you arrived, and the unshakable feeling that you might have killed something far beyond your understanding. Flemethâs place in the Dragon Age universe was too significant to be silenced by something as trivial as death, but for a moment, you feel like you have driven a stake through the heart of something you cannot comprehend.

Dragon Age: Originsâ big moment where all your choices culminate is The Landsmeet, a political meeting where you can finally unmask Loghain for all his crimes and essentially set up the country of Fereldenâs future. Your relationships and understandings formed over the past 50+ hours of video game are put to the test, and things can change drastically depending on how the battles of wits and blades pan out. To this day, The Landsmeet is one of BioWareâs most effective showcases of its ability to sew hours of choices into a final consequence. In just one quest you solidify the future for Ferelden in a way that sends most players down the same path, but colors that result so differently that many players, especially those who donât know every secret the game has to offer, will see something that diverges significantly from what the next player might see.

One of the last major choices youâll make in Dragon Age: Origins comes back to Morrigan. The witch has had more than enough reasons to leave the party considering she doesnât really get along with anyone on the team, but she sticks around long enough to give you a final choice: ending the Blight will cost you your lifeâunless you or Alistair undergoes a blood magic ritual that will transfer the Archdemonâs soul into an unborn child. It sounds like a get-out-of-jail-free card, all you have to do is lay with her for one night or convince Alistair to do it. But Morrigan is cagey with her intentions and says that whether you agree or not, she will leave the party after the final battle. This is why sheâs been here this whole time, but does that mean any connection youâve formed with her was all an act? What will become of this child? Is it going to be like any other child or will it be some darkspawn demon that could bring about just as much pain in the world as the archdemon would? Morrigan gives you nothing to go on, but makes her terms clear. Dragon Age: Origins would go on to have three sequels that would wipe away the ambiguity of this decision, but at the time, all you had to go on here was your trust of Morrigan, or lack thereof. Everything youâve ever been told about blood magic and interrupting the natural order of the Blight should tell you to say âno,â but are you willing to risk it to save your own life? Itâs a fascinating choice. Did Dragon Age do right by it? Your mileage may vary.

With Dragon Age II, BioWare started earnestly looking for a way to franchise the series. It had built itself a new cage as the âchoice and consequenceâ studio thanks to the Mass Effect series, and Dragon Age followed suit by importing your Origins save to pepper in cameos and references to your past deeds. That includes whether or not you killed Flemeth, but since BioWare still wanted to use the mysterious witch either way, it had new hero Hawke unwittingly carry her to safety through an enchanted amulet even as she fought for her life against the Hero of Ferelden. Reviving Flemeth is one of the most effective moments in all of Dragon Age in showing how playing as different protagonists in each game could create satisfying meta moments. As she rises from the ashes, you watch the impact of one of your heroâs actions be undermined by the one youâre playing as now. Dragon Age takes place over decades, and a big part of its appeal is watching different stories youâve helped write weave in and out of one another. Itâs a course correction, but one that is still bone-chilling to watch unfold.

The second Dragon Age differs from the first in several ways, from taking place almost entirely in one city to swapping the tactical RPG battle system for more action-oriented combat. But one of the most notable and interesting changes it made was to the approval system, which integrated a Friendship and Rivalry mechanic so you didnât have to kiss a party memberâs ass to progress their relationship storyline. The difference between Friendship and Rivalry is all about how you challenge their preconceived notions. Each party member has a pretty defined view of the world; the radical mage Anders, for instance, is all about freeing magic users from the Circle at any cost, while the elven slave Fenris has an aversion to magic. Uncritically enabling them will give you Friendship points, and going against the grain will net you Rivalry points. This changes the tone of your relationships significantly, and even someone youâre in a romantic relationship with may greet you with a thorny disposition. Watching those connections gradually change is one of the most compelling parts of Dragon Age IIâs writing. Romancing Fenris as a mage while being rivals was one of the most interesting, angsty relationships Iâve ever experienced in a BioWare game. Itâs a shame the studio didnât keep the system around.

Dragon Age II is all about years of civil unrest bubbling to the surface of one city, and between the conflict with the stranded Qunari and the Mage/Templar War, the former is certainly handled with more care than the latter. While early Dragon Age games had multiple crisis points in which party members can leave the party or betray you, one of the most memorable is when one party member makes a decision not to leave, but to return. Isabela is the cause of the Qunariâs extended stay in Kirkwall, and when sheâs given the chance to run off with a tome they have been searching for, she takes it. If youâve not established a solid enough friendship or rivalry with her, she will never return. If you have, she makes a big heroâs entrance just as the Qunari are about to strike down what remains of the city. She attempts to make amends, showing the growth sheâs been trying her damnedest to avoid since arriving in the city. But then the Qunari leader says she still must answer for her crimes. You can give her up and betray her, or you can fight for her instead, and seeing her be big enough to not sell you and the rest of Kirkwall out for once in her life is one of Dragon Age IIâs most memorable companion moments.

Choosing to fight for Isabelaâs freedom results in a somewhat silly but exceptionally satisfying fight. Dragon Age IIâs action-based combat isnât quite as snappy and tight as The Veilguardâs, but it has some spectacle that can keep it interesting in fights that donât just pit you against waves of enemies being thrown at you. The Arishok fight can go a few ways depending on if he respects Hawke or not, but fighting the giant Qunari in a one-on-one duel is still one of the best combat sequences in the game. You may be in for a tough time if you havenât specâd into a class and build that can handle a solo fight, but in any case, taking down the Arishok and being crowned the Champion of Kirkwall is one of the defining moments of Dragon Age II

One bright spot in Dragon Age IIâs extremely uneven final act is the conclusion to Merrillâs story. The elven blood mage has gone against the wishes of everyone around her in a tunnel-visioned need to bring back a part of her clanâs history, even seeking out the help of a demon. Dragon Age II takes place across a decade, with Merrill at odds with her clan leader Marethari all the while, and yet the leader sacrifices herself to âsaveâ Merrill by allowing the demon she had been working with to possess her instead. Merrill can insist this was meddling and you can be supportive of her or not, but the real people she has to answer to are the clanâs remaining members. Depending on whether you advocate for her or throw her under the bus, you may have to fight the entire clan on your way out. Itâs a brutal mess thatâs tied to the character with perhaps the most emotional range of any party member in the franchise. Itâs such a terrifying, saddening web of contradicting feelings and subverted expectations, all leading to a stunning payoff.

I have a lot of issues with the handling of the Mage/Templar War in Dragon Age II. It creates this complicated political and religious conflict around an oppressed group of people and a tyrannical religious organization but insists that both sides are equally bad, actually. Donât even get me started on how you can convince Anders, the radical mage who is the face of this conflict, to kill the mages he tried to save. But the moment in which Anders, worn down by a lifetime of captivity and oppression, blows up the Kirkwall Chantry is one of the few unambiguous statements the game makes in its final hours. The scene itself is dramatic and shocking and kickstarts a war that would (in theory) shake the foundations of Thedas. It requires everyone in your party to make a stand. There will be no more fence-sitting in this fight, and all your relationships will be tested as your team decides whether or not to follow you into battle. Sadly, the reveals that follow undermine any choice you make, but as a spark that ignites a flame, Andersâ act of terrorism is a statement in a game that otherwise seems unwilling to make one.

A lot of the highlights weâve talked about are big story moments or reactions to your decisions, but one of the coolest things Inquisition does happens literally the moment the game starts. The main menu shows rows of mages and templars marching toward a building off in the distance. Despite where we left them in Dragon Age II, these two opposing sides donât seem to be fighting, so perhaps theyâre making their way to peace talks? Could the future of Dragon Age be written not in blood, but in signed treaties? Letâs press ânew gameâ and find o-

I have heard some fans say the moment in which members of the Inquisition start singing âThe Dawn Will Come,â a hymn of the Chantry, to your main character in a moment of religious fervor is cheesy and cringe, to which I say, fuck you, itâs one of the most incredible moments in the game. Inquisitionâs themes can be radically different depending on how you play the Herald of Andraste. This hero has been unwillingly made a religious figure, with hundreds of people expecting you to live as a symbol for a god you might not even believe in. If you take this approach, playing as a non-believer who actively shouts down the claims of the faithful, âThe Dawn Will Comeâ can be an unnerving, haunting reminder of how much unwavering belief can compel groups of people even as you insist on a different, provable truth. If, on the other hand, youâre undecided or playing as a believer, it can read like a beautiful moment of hope and community. Inquisition allows you to define so many shades of who your character is and see them reflected in a world that struggles with your very existence. And sometimes, no matter how hard you kick and scream, you cannot stop the world from believing what it does. Instead, you can just awkwardly stand there while people sing to you and then complain about it later.

With each subsequent game, Dragon Age has gotten better at illustrating the closeness (or lack thereof) of your companions. Banter in the overworld is good, but seeing the crew actually get together is better. The Wicked Grace scene, in which the party gets together to play a card game, is one of BioWareâs best scenes that make use of a gameâs entire core ensemble. Everyoneâs personality gets a chance to shine, whether theyâre playful, stuffy, horny, or just trying to wrangle all these weirdos together. Itâs delightful, succinct, and has stayed in the hearts of many Dragon Age fans.

The Dragon Age series has always been explicitly queer. For all the diaper-shitting about The Veilguardâs queer themes, Inquisition was examining the life and times of a Thedas gay long before Taash learned the term ânon-binary.â Dorian Pavusâ personal quest remains one of the most memorable in all of BioWareâs canon. It drops combat for one incredibly well-acted cutscene between the Tevinter mage and his estranged father, where itâs revealed that, to continue their bloodline and climb his way up the Tevinter political ladder, Dorianâs father planned to use a blood magic equivalent to conversion therapy in order to force his son into an arranged marriage. Iâve spoken to many Dragon Age fans over the years about what decision they made here, as youâre able to help the two reconcile, or to get Dorian out of there. Iâve never once considered telling Dorian to hear his father out. Itâs one of the best examples Iâve seen of a game adapting the queer struggle to a fictional culture. Dorian becomes a radical because he has seen how low even those he loves will go to maintain power in Tevinter, and it all ties into his identity as a gay man. Itâs a stunning scene that tells you so much about Dorian and where he came from, and lets you gently nudge history as you stand beside him.

Blackwall goes under the radar for a lot of players. Heâs quiet, keeps to himself, and is even in a pretty out-of-the-way spot in your base in Skyhold. A lot of people think the Grey Warden warrior is boring, but theyâre wrong; the big reveals you experience in his companion missions are outstanding. Blackwall tells you heâs a Warden but is secretive about the organization which, if you played Origins, may nudge you to think back to your own experience playing as one. You know why theyâre all tight-lipped on the inner machinations of the faction, so you donât question it. But it turns out, heâs actually not a Warden at all, and is instead an imposter on the run for war crimes he committed years ago. Eventually, the guilt eats at him and he turns himself in to save others from answering for his orders with a hangmanâs noose. This man duped you for dozens of hours, and youâre left with the power to decide his fate. Blackwallâs quest can go one of several ways, whether you leave him to rot, pardon him, or send him to the Wardens to let them decide what happens to an imposter. Whatever you choose, Blackwallâs quest leaves an impression as one of BioWareâs most surprising and subversive. Yâall need to quit calling characters you donât even talk to boring. This shit rips.

Even as someone who likes Mass Effect more than Dragon Age, I have a hard time thinking of a singular quest in the sci-fi series that matches up to Inquisitionâs Wicked Eyes and Wicked Hearts. While you will unsheathe your weapons a few times, this mission is all about politics, charming the worst people youâve ever met, and working the crowd. Running around the Winter Palace, meeting the most powerful players in Orlais, and manipulating the politics of an entire country to your whims is more intriguing than anything you do with a sword or staff. Mechanically, the mission is surprisingly elegant as it codifies social status and attention into something that can be measured by a video game, and itâs intriguing learning more about the figureheads you can rally to your cause. There are several outcomes at the end of this mission, and getting what you want might come down to blackmail, reuniting long-lost lovers, or a betrayal of your own. Itâs unlike anything else in the Dragon Age series, and I havenât seen many studios pull off something like it since.

At one point, it seemed as if Flemeth might be the throughline connecting all of Dragon Age. For two games, she was presented as a manipulator, lurking in the shadows and moving the pieces of Thedasâ chess board to her liking. Then all her machinations finally came to a head in Inquisition when she, Morrigan, and perhaps the child the player helped conceive two games prior, all gather in the Fade. Flemeth seemingly has control of the situation, appearing to hold her grandson Kieran hostage and using him as leverage against her daughter who has been on the run since Origins. But as anger gives way to truth-telling and the moment softens, the two find not total reconciliation, but at least an understanding that neither is in danger from the other. It is a series-best performance from Black and Flemeth actor Kate Mulgrew, bringing together three games of choices and history into one incredible confrontation. Iâm still unsure how I feel about the final echoes of this moment in The Veilguard, but Flemeth and her family reuniting and acknowledging the struggle of love and fear for one another that theyâre caught in remains one of the most memorable interactions in all of Dragon Age

I could just throw the entirety of the Trespasser DLC in here and it would be in the running for best âmomentsâ in the series. The final expansion BioWare released for Inquisition in 2015 isnât just an epilogue for the RPG, but is pretty much the true ending. You say goodbye to all the companions with some silly, heartfelt scenes, engage in some politics, and fight some really memorable battles, but the meat of the DLC is in its final 10 minutes. Solas, the elven apostate who abandons your team at the very end, reveals that he is the Dread Wolf, the trickster god who led a rebellion against the rest of the elven pantheon. He plans to tear down the barrier between the real and spirit worlds, which he believes will revitalize the old world of the elves, granting them immortality once more and destroying everyone else in the process. But youâre given two choices that (before The Veilguard, at least) felt incredibly meaningful as a final word for the Inquisitor: Do you think Solas is beyond saving? And is your organization in a state to fight him? Ultimately, neither of those choices mattered in The Veilguard, despite them being imported into the game at the beginning. But back in 2015 it felt like a victory lap, a final declaration by a character you probably wouldnât get to play again.

BioWare has always been held up as a studio that spearheads inclusive design, but The Veilguard takes this one step further by letting you explicitly determine that your protagonist Rook is trans. This isnât just a cosmetic choice like giving them top surgery scars or picking a voice; it can be part of your characterâs backstory that you talk about from time to time with other characters. Few games have been this thorough about letting you define your characterâs identity, and The Veilguard approaches it with a great deal of care.

The Veilguard continues the trend, started with Mass Effect: Andromeda, of BioWare hiding some of a gameâs biggest lore reveals behind an optional collectathon, but this time they are so far-reaching and important that I canât believe some players may never see them. Collecting wolf statues throughout The Veilguard reveals Solasâ regrets. These are murals depicting memories from the elven godâs long life, and essentially write the creation myth of the Dragon Age universe. When I first played The Veilguard, I did these quests pretty late and they started to turn me around on the game entirely. I had mostly considered The Veilguard less a meal than a series of really good sides, but this was when I as a long-time fan felt like I was really eating. Each reveal was juicier and more surprising than the last, bringing connective tissue to a universe that had often felt disparate and disconnected. God, I canât believe theyâre optional.

A lot of The Veilguardâs choices are binary, but most of them are still pretty compelling. The first world-altering choice comes when you must decide which of two cities to save from incoming dragon attacks: Minrathous or Treviso. Thereâs a lot of emotion tied up in this choice, as well as tactical considerations to make. Your Rook might be from Minrathous, but pursuing a relationship with Treviso native Lucanis. You may be trying to develop partnerships with the radical Tevinter group the Shadow Dragons and feel like you should help them defend their city to not burn bridges. Whatever your reasoning and whatever the consequences, you have to choose right then and there. Your teammates are looking to you for an answer, and you realize that a mere few hours of gameplay ago you were just a contractor helping Varric track down Solas. Rookâs arc is all about them confronting the leadership role that has been thrust on them by circumstance and Varricâs expectations. This is the moment it becomes clear that they might not be cut out for the decisions they have to make, but theyâll have to learn to live with those choices one way or another.

The Mourn Watch necromancer Emmrich is The Veilguardâs best marriage of character and faction culture. He is fascinated by death because he has an all-consuming fear of the end. Emmrichâs goal is to become a Lich, an immortal keeper of the dead, willing to watch life begin and end forevermore. But as his personal quests unfold, his assistant Manfred, a reanimated skeleton, is killed in a battle with a rival Lich. Using his powers, he could bring Manfred back, but doing so would disqualify him from achieving the immortality he desires, as it would show an inability to accept death. How can you be immortal and watch everything live and die in an endless cycle if one death of a loved one compels you to defy the natural order? Iâve heard people make cases for allowing Emmrich to become a Lich, but I chose to advise him to bring Manfred back and leave Lichdom behind. The Lich order may believe his inability to leave Manfred behind as a weakness, but I saw it as an asset. Itâs proof that he loves too strongly to spend an eternity watching everyone he cares about disappear over and over again. Still, I see the argument for the other side. No other choice in The Veilguard so succinctly nails the companion-first format BioWare wanted while saying so much about the world in the process.

The Grey Warden headquarters of Weisshaupt has been referenced since the very beginning of Dragon Age, and after all those years hyping it up, our first experience of it is one hell of a followthrough. The Veilguardâs mission at the fortress is an action-packed and narratively rewarding setpiece packed with reveals about the state of the Grey Wardens and demonstrating just how much of a threat the remaining elven gods pose. Meanwhile, the drama it stirs between your team of usually harmonious heroes is a peak moment for the whole series, and holy shit, that boss fight at the end might be the most challenging BioWareâs ever created.

After you see all of Solasâ regrets, you meet a visitor in the Lighthouse: Morrigan. She gives you one last big lore dump, finally putting a bittersweet bow on the tragic story between her and her mother. She also reveals to you that the figure that has been looming over their hit-and-run relationship is Mythal, the elven god of love who once led the pantheon. Mythal is long dead, but her memories have transferred from host to host in the millennia since. Morrigan is the keeper of her memories now, and believes that if even a fraction of the old god were able to release Solas from all his regret, it might be enough to take him off this violent path. Morriganâs epilogue is introspective and melancholy, but as she directs you to one of the last pieces of Mythalâs soul trapped in the fade, all that family drama is given some meaning. The conversation in which you try to convince Mythal to help you is one of the best in The Veilguard. It branches into multiple topics, giving you several footholds to perhaps convince her that your cause is just. Who your Rook is can play into how effective you are in making your case, and if you canât persuade her, you can always fight her for her favor. Whatever route you choose, this is one of those moments in which you can feel Dragon Age history changing with every dialogue option you pick.

Dragon Age: The Veilguardâs final missions are a kind of greatest hits of BioWareâs best tricks. Itâs got everything: unavoidable sacrifice, avoidable losses determined by whether or not you know your team well enough to assign them tasks befitting their talents, and a culmination of all the strategic relationships youâve built with different factions. It might not be as interactive as Mass Effect 2âs Suicide Mission, but as a series of interlocking decisions bringing you to a myriad of mini conclusions, it far exceeds anything the studio has done in the past 20 years. I was nervous and shaking making those choices, and itâs all portrayed with a level of cinematic finesse that goes beyond anything BioWareâs done before.

When The Veilguard reaches its climax, it becomes clear that all the while, youâve been caught in a battle of ideals between Varricâs hope and Solasâ cynicism. Rook has been a pawn (no pun intended) for Solas. The elf has been manipulating them the entire time in hopes of trapping them in the Fade and resuming his plan. Heâs done this by projecting a vision of Varric who hypes Rook up until they can be cut off at the knees, falling into a state of regret so consuming it traps them within the spirit realm. Here, theyâre guided by Varric through the prison until they discover the truth: Varric died at the beginning of the game, and Solas used his image to nudge Rook along the entire game.

The reveal is incredible because you realize BioWare pulled off a Sixth Sense. No one else speaks to Varric the entire game, but heâs placed naturally enough in each scene that you donât really question that no one else responds to him. You realize that youâve been fooled by Solas just as much as Rook has, and when they mourn their mentorâs loss, theyâre effectively a stand-in for you, the Dragon Age fan. But as despondent as they might be, they still have a job to do, and Varric reminds them that theyâve done everything up to this point by themself. They donât need Varricâs guidance. They already have everything they need.

As frustrated as I was with The Veilguardâs decision to leave the Inquisitor behind for a new protagonist, this twist was what made Rook work for me. The whole game essentially emerges from Varric betting on someone to finish the job he couldnât. His belief in Rook is what keeps the game going, even as Solas tries to manipulate it to his own advantage. It may have been sad to watch Varric go from a city dwarf just trying to make it to a victim of Solasâ pride, but his belief in others lives on.

After four games, pretty much everything Dragon Age has ever been leads to one final conversation with Solas. The Veil is coming down, the rest of Thedas will be burned to ash in the aftermath, and the only way to stop it is for the trickster god himself to bind himself to it. No matter what you do, Solas will end up using his immortal life force to keep Thedas and the Fade separate. But the tenor of your decision still matters. You can knock him senseless and forcibly cast the blood magic spell to hold him there, you can trick him so his magic backfires and leave him helpless as you bind him to the Veil, or you can take the third option. Bringing Mythalâs essence out allows her to release him from her service, letting him lay down a lifetime of regret. Itâs the culmination of learning all the secrets left in this world, and once you have all that understanding, it feels like the most appropriate way to cap off a cliffhanger whose resolution weâve been awaiting for ten years.

Given everything thatâs happened to BioWare in the years following The Veilguardâs launch, what sticks out to me most is how much the game leans into finality. Closure is a key pillar of its storytelling, even if there are hints of a sequel we’ll never get. And if this is the note we had to leave it off on, I’m not upset. I hope the folks who were at BioWare at any point during the seriesâ development aren’t either.

Sony Pushes PS5 Owners To Trade In Consoles Amid Unprecedented Price Hikes

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Sony pursues new trade-in options as prices for the PS5 surge

The future of affordable video game consoles is not looking good, and hardware makers like Sony know it. The PlayStation 5 has undergone two major price hikes while the Xbox Series X has jumped in price three times in a single year. The AI-driven VRAM crisis at the heart of the issue is expected to worsen. Given the supply constraints, Sony has limited options for selling PS5s at prices customers might find acceptable.

It doesn't seem like a coincidence, then, that some PS5 owners have started receiving notifications directly from Sony about a new partnership with the tech sustainability company Back Market. The company advocates ending ‘fast tech’ and operates, among other services, a marketplace for refurbished electronics.

According to Sony, current PS5 owners can receive up to $400 for their old consoles on Back Market — provided the hardware is in good condition and the user includes two controllers. That's more money than competitors like GameStop offer. At the same time, when used or refurbished PS5s sell somewhere between $600 and $1,300, Sony's offer may not be the most appealing deal for most consumers. This may appeal mainly to users who planned to upgrade anyway — a group that is growing as the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 nears.

Like Sony, Xbox has spent part of 2026 trying to encourage its fans to trade in their consoles for cash. Microsoft frames it as a pragmatic option for users who aren’t using their consoles — an unintended acknowledgment of Xbox’s weaker sales pitch this generation. More recently, and to the skepticism of many, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma claimed that demand for Xbox consoles has exceeded supply; she proposed mitigating the issue with an expansion of Xbox's refurbishment program.

The timing of both programs coincides with the imminent release of major games like GTA 6 and the holiday season, when consoles are in demand. How this plays out remains to be seen. Given the PlayStation 6's rumored exorbitant price tag and the sudden explosion around the PS5's jailbreak, some users might have extra incentive to hold onto their old consoles.

Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop.

Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months.

This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network.

The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program.

In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware.

That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto.

Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft.

The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems.

These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.

By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.”

But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention.

While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise.

Binance spokesperson Ross O’Leary referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack.

The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident.

The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history.

Google is cutting schools off from Search if they restrict AI

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Google is turning off Gemini and Search by default for K-12 student accounts until school administrators enable them

David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Google $GOOGL is cutting off K-12 student access to Google Search at schools that do not enable its Gemini AI products, according to NBC News. The company announced the changes to its education products on Tuesday, including updated controls for Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom and Google Search.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, wrote in a blog post that access to those products "will be entirely off for K-12 student accounts until school administrators explicitly turn them on," according to NBC News. Before Tuesday's change, Gemini was switched on by default in any school that used Google Classroom.

"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Phillips wrote, according to NBC News.

Google said it is bringing Guided Learning to Google Classroom globally and adding Guided Learning capabilities to Google Search. Administrators who activate Search can also enable a "guided learning mode" that recognizes when a student drops homework questions into the search box, according to The Wall Street Journal. Under that setting, the chatbot is built to walk students through a problem one stage at a time without handing over the final answer.

Districts that offer Search cannot fully turn off its AI Overview and AI Mode features, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, criticized the decision. "It is unfortunate that Google has prioritized its business interests over the education of our children," she told NBC News. Josh Golin, executive director of the advocacy group Fairplay, described Google's approach in a statement as an effort to "strong-arm schools into using its AI products," according to NBC News.

The change follows pressure over Google's AI tools in classrooms. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, and Sen. Josh Hawley, a Missouri Republican, sent a letter to Google CEO Sundar Pichai asking what the company knows about how its AI products affect children's mental health and learning. They set a Nov. 2 deadline for a reply.

The senators cited a September investigation by The Wall Street Journal, which relied on more than 60 interviews with clinicians, parents, students, school officials and educators. It found that many students had come to lean on Google's AI tools for both their schoolwork and their emotional needs.

In early October, 13 parent advocacy organizations, including the Digital Childhood Institute and Schools Beyond Screens, sent an open letter urging districts to disable student use of both Gemini and YouTube, according to NBC News.

Apple Opens Siri AI Developer Preview for Custom App Integrations

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

Apple announced on November 3, 2026 that its Siri AI Developer Preview is open to all developers through the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas. Apps can expose custom content and actions through App Intents, allowing Siri AI to handle requests such as checking deliveries, booking reservations, and placing orders.

The opening extends Siri AI beyond actions and data that fit Apple’s system-defined app schemas. Integrations can draw on personal-context understanding and onscreen awareness, letting people phrase requests in their own words, and Siri AI can surface any entity in Spotlight’s semantic index rather than only entities matching an existing schema. Apple has begun rolling out related capabilities across its own apps, including Calendar, Files, Mail, Maps, Messages, Photos, and Shortcuts; examples include finding a previously visited coffee shop and archiving files unopened for more than a year.

Under the Developer Preview documentation, invocation depends on context. A person does not need to name an app while it is in the foreground, while a Live Activity is active, or when continuing a Siri conversation that already included the app. Background requests require the app’s name. For example, a ride-hailing customer could follow a Live Activity and then ask Siri to change the pickup address without restating the app.

Siri AI can also find content in one app, transfer it to a specified second app, and perform an action there. Apple’s example sends a user’s favorite sneakers through a messaging app after resolving the recipient through Contacts. Requested custom content can appear in developer-supplied card snippets that use the app’s own views and branding. No new entitlement or separate developer program is required.

Apple’s implementation guidance makes exposure selective: developers decide which content Siri may retrieve and which actions it may perform. A Swift macro, @AppIntent(.tool), turns a new or existing custom intent into a tool Siri can call. Intents already conforming to a Siri-supported schema in a primary domain do not need that annotation.

Titles and descriptions for intents, parameters, and entity properties help Siri interpret natural-language wording, distinguish similar actions, and formulate responses. Developers can index entities in Spotlight, associate visible app content with entities for onscreen context, and donate intents when users perform matching actions to supply behavioral cues. Transferable representations allow custom entities to move between apps during cross-app requests.

Access can be narrowed for sensitive data. Authentication policies can protect an entire entity or selected properties, while an internal visibility setting prevents Siri, Shortcuts, and other system features from reading a property. Apple’s finance example requires authentication for an account nickname and balance but keeps the routing number internal to the app and its extensions.

For multi-step work, app skills supplement individual tool intents. A skill is a Markdown file whose metadata helps Siri decide whether it matches a request; Siri consults the instruction body only after making that match. The instructions can describe action order, which intent to prefer, practices to avoid, app-specific domain knowledge, and when to ask clarifying questions. A shopping skill could coordinate searching for items, adding them to a cart, choosing payment and delivery methods, reviewing the cart, and confirming the purchase.

Xcode’s Siri Integration Advisor offers implementation feedback, and the Siri Evaluations framework lets developers script requests, measure responses, and detect changes as intents and entities evolve. Developers can run development-signed builds on supported devices and share them with internal TestFlight testers. External TestFlight testers cannot use the preview, and its functionality does not work in App Store versions even when those apps contain the new integration.

Apple says the first customer release is expected in a few months, with App Store submissions scheduled to open in the spring. Further terms and usage policies for Siri AI-enabled experiences will follow. Siri AI requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language. It is available in English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, with Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese listed as forthcoming.

Siri AI is unavailable in the EU on iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS, and Apple says it is working with the EU on a possible route to availability. It is not available to users under 13, and some features may not be available in every region or language.

Certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models, including Siri AI, are subject to daily usage limits. Apple says expanded access to those features will be available for a fee in the future.

The immediate change is a build-and-test opening rather than a full customer release. Developers can define the data and actions Siri AI may use, orchestrate them across workflows, and evaluate the results internally, while customer availability, App Store submissions, and detailed usage policies remain tied to later stages of Apple’s rollout.

Social Security COLA, tax break could narrow spending gap for older consumers in 2027

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

A Bank of America Institute report finds baby boomer and traditionalist households have weaker discretionary spending growth than other generations despite large wealth gains among the richest older households. Because many retirees rely on fixed income sources and benefit less from recent wage growth, their budgets have been under pressure. A temporary federal tax deduction for those 65 and older and a 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 could modestly improve real incomes, particularly if inflation cools as forecast.   AI Summary

The spending growth of older consumers has trailed other age groups for the past year despite sizable wealth gains at the top. But a 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients and temporary tax break could modestly improve their purchasing power, according to a Bank of America Institute report released last week.

Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card data to show that baby boomer and traditionalist households have posted weaker discretionary spending growth than other Americans for roughly a year. That marks a reversal from 2022 and 2023, when older households were outpacing others. Boomers were defined as those born between 1946 and 1964, while traditionalists are those born before 1946.

The report ties part of this slowdown to how wealth is distributed within the older cohorts. Using 2025 data from the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, the bank found that about two-thirds of net wealth among households headed by someone older than 65 is held by the top 10% of these households. This concentration means that stock market and asset gains may do little to support spending for most older consumers.

Overall consumer spending strength in 2026 appears to be driven primarily by wage and salary growth, particularly among lower- and middle-income working households. Older households, by contrast, depend on a broader mix of income sources and are less exposed to accelerating wages.

Fed survey data shows that as households age, a smaller share of income comes from wages or self-employment and more from pensions, Social Security, and interest, dividends or rental income. Bank of America’s internal data highlight the resulting divergence within older cohorts: Households over 62 that rely only on Social Security have average income and discretionary spending close to half that of their peers who drawing from Social Security, pensions and employment combined.

Discretionary spending is also more uneven across income tiers for older generations than for all households. Retirees are the least likely group to expect their finances to improve over the next six months, according to the study, reflecting the challenges of living on largely fixed income sources.

The report points to two policy levers that could support older consumers’ budgets in the near term:

COLAs are based on the year-over-year change in the third quarter for the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). While these increases are designed to preserve purchasing power, they can be more or less generous depending on the inflation path in the year that follows.

In 2022, for example, inflation slowed sharply after a large COLA took effect, effectively boosting real benefits and helping older generations outspend other age cohorts in 2022 and 2023.

Consensus forecasts cited in the Bank of America report anticipate that overall inflation will cool in 2027, largely as the impact of higher gasoline prices fades. If that occurs, the 3.6% COLA could outpace actual price increases next year, delivering a more meaningful real income gain for households heavily reliant on Social Security.

The survey data shows that the largest spending growth gaps between older generations and all households are concentrated in discretionary categories like electronics, lodging, restaurants, clothing, furniture and airlines. In many of these areas, older cohorts’ year-over-year spending growth lags the overall population by several percentage points.

Some of this pattern likely reflects differences in preferences and life stages. But if Social Security benefits rise faster than prices in 2027 and the tax deduction continues to support middle-income seniors, the report suggests there may be room for older households’ discretionary spending growth to narrow the gap with other age groups.

CrowdStrike Adds AI Kill Switch to Falcon Guardian for Rogue Agents

📅 Nov 03, 2026  |  Category: Technology  |  Read Source →

CrowdStrike announced the AI Kill Switch for Falcon Guardian on November 3, 2026, giving security teams a human-controlled way to interrupt rogue AI agents. The feature is available at launch and uses connected AI gateways to deny agents access to AI models.

The launch addresses agents that can chain tasks and operate with system-level access across endpoints, cloud environments and SaaS applications. CrowdStrike says these agents can encounter obstacles and take actions no one authorized, even when no adversary is involved. The kill switch requires an authorized administrator to trigger the response, and every action is recorded in an audit trail.

Enforcement runs through either the generally available Falcon AI Gateway or a third-party AI gateway already in use. The CrowdStrike gateway is included with Guardian at no additional cost. It consolidates model access, security policies, credential management, and usage and cost controls in the Falcon platform. CrowdStrike says the gateway also extends protection to applications and workloads outside direct endpoint-sensor coverage, including unmanaged environments.

The Guardian product documentation defines the current response as centralized enforcement that cuts access to designated AI models and providers, with gateway enforcement by agent type marked as coming soon. The immediate control therefore concerns the agent’s connection to AI services, a narrower mechanism than the name might suggest.

Falcon Guardian itself has been generally available since September 2026, so the kill switch extends an existing product. Guardian already discovers enterprise AI agents, enforces policies on their actions and detects attacks against them. CrowdStrike Agent Graph links an agent’s instructions to subsequent execution and the identities, tools, systems and resources involved, allowing investigators to trace both activity and impact.

CrowdStrike’s rationale for combining these control points is that agent-level and network-only views leave different blind spots. The company says agent-level hooks see prompts but can miss model responses and some actions, while network-only tools cannot observe host execution or local and open-weight models whose activity never crosses the network. Guardian combines agent hooks, endpoint network inspection and endpoint runtime visibility on one Falcon sensor. Endpoint network inspection is generally available for Windows and in early access for Mac.

The launch announcement presents a broader response: terminating an agent where it runs, blocking relaunches on a targeted host or host group, and removing its enterprise network access. Its own availability sequence puts termination first at the gateway and soon on the endpoint. Direct termination of endpoint agents and their associated processes, as well as prevention of restarts, are part of the coming-soon expansion beyond gateway enforcement.

Planned coordinated containment also covers terminating or containing cloud agents, revoking agent permissions at runtime, restricting or ending agent activity in SaaS environments, and terminating browser sessions. Charlotte Agentic SOAR is intended to coordinate those enforcement points and enable automated kill-switch workflows triggered by AI-specific detections or risky agent behavior. CrowdStrike says the expansion is designed to target individual agents or groups while minimizing disruption to broader business operations.

The launch separates two questions that the term kill switch can blur: whether security teams can immediately deny an agent its model connection, and whether they can disable the agent’s processes and permissions wherever it operates. The shipping control addresses the first through gateways; the second depends on coordinated enforcement that remains on CrowdStrike’s roadmap.
